# Potluck

> Potluck is free, open-source software (Apache-2.0) that puts a team's idle Macs and Linux machines to work: self-hosted GitHub Actions runners and sandboxes for coding agents, each job in a fresh VM or sandbox that is thrown away afterwards. It is made by Sengi.

Potluck is a program (`potluck`) for macOS and Linux. One machine runs a pool; friends and teammates join with a one-time code and lend machines to it. Work goes to a machine that is free, and a machine's owner can take it back at any time. There are no accounts: machines find each other over Tailscale (or a tunnel you set up).

- Install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh`
- Source, issues and documentation: https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck
- Releases: https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/releases
- Mezze, mail and work items for teams of coding agents, a separate product from the same makers that runs on Potluck: https://mezze.sh/
- Maker: Sengi, https://sengi.run

---

Source: https://potluck.sh/

# Put your team's idle machines to work.

Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners and sandboxes for coding agents, each job in a fresh VM or sandbox, on the Macs and Linux boxes you already own. When someone needs their machine back, it's theirs. Free and open source (Apache-2.0).

Install on macOS or Linux:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
```

Free and open source (Apache-2.0) · macOS and Linux. Code: https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck

## Got an invite code?

Someone sent you a code to their pool. Install Potluck (above), then:

```sh
potluck join '<code>'
potluck sandbox create
```

`potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a` runs a command in it; `potluck sandbox rm <id>` ends it; `potluck leave` leaves the pool. A code sent for sharing your machine (`potluck invite <you> --host`) goes to `potluck host '<code>'` instead. You need only Potluck, even when the pool runs on Mezze.

## Or have your coding agent set it up

Copy this prompt into Claude Code, Codex or any coding agent, and it sets Potluck up on that machine.

```text
Set up Potluck (https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck) on this machine so I can try it alone. Read https://potluck.sh/llms-full.txt first. Then:
1. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh (if it says ~/.local/bin is not on PATH, run the line it prints).
2. Run `potluck doctor` and tell me what is missing. On a Mac that is usually Tart, Softnet and about 60 GB of free disk. Show me any sudo line it prints; do not run sudo yourself.
3. When doctor is clean: potluck create trial --via tunnel, then potluck host --reclaim-idle-s 0 (on a Mac the first run pulls about 27 GB).
4. potluck sandbox create, then potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a, then potluck sandbox rm <id>.
Stop and ask me before anything that needs a password, a sign-in or deleting files. If a command fails, show me its exact output.
```

## How it works

One machine runs the pool. Everyone else brings theirs. Work goes to whichever machine is free, and each job gets a fresh VM or sandbox that is thrown away after.

1. **Lay out the blanket.** On one machine, start a pool for your team (`potluck create friends`) and make invite codes (`potluck invite sam --host`). Potluck has no accounts of its own. Your machines find each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you set up with `--via tunnel`.
2. **Friends bring their machines.** Bring every computer you can spare: the old gaming PC, the Mac mini, the rented server, a cloud VM with hours left over. Put each one in one pool or several. A machine joins only if its checks pass (`potluck doctor`, then `potluck host <code>`).
3. **Leo wants his Mac back.** A Mac works for the team only while its owner is away: when the owner touches the keyboard or trackpad, the job on the Mac ends, and nothing new starts until it has been idle for five minutes (`potluck host --reclaim-idle-s` changes that; 0 shares all the time). To get a machine back for good, `potluck host set drain` winds it down and `potluck host set closed` stops it now.

## What you can do with it

- **Coding agents: give your agent a computer of its own.** An agent's commands run in a throwaway sandbox on a pool machine, not on your laptop: `potluck sandbox create`, `potluck sandbox exec <id> -- make test`, `potluck sandbox rm <id>`. Or hand the agent the sandbox tools over MCP with `{"mcpServers":{"potluck":{"command":"potluck","args":["mcp"]}}}`. To run Claude Code's self-hosted runner in fresh sandboxes: `potluck agent-runner claude --secret-file <key-file> --image ghcr.io/sengirunners/potluck-box-agent`.
- **GitHub Actions: move a macOS job onto your own Mac.** `potluck ci pr acme/app` prepares a change to one line of your workflow (`runs-on: macos-15` becomes your Mac, with GitHub's runner kept for forks); then you open the pull request it prepares. Pull requests from forks keep using GitHub's runner.

At GitHub's listed rate for its standard macOS runner ($0.062 a minute as of November 2026), 5,000 macOS GitHub Actions minutes a month on a private repository, after your plan's included minutes, cost $310. On your own Mac with Potluck they cost nothing but electricity. Public repositories run on GitHub's runners for free.

## House rules

- **Work stays in a box.** Every job runs in a throwaway VM or sandbox, not directly on your machine, and is deleted after.
- **Keys go only where you send them.** A job gets a secret only when you grant it, only on a friend's machine, and as a file: never on the command line or in its environment.
- **Friends and strangers.** Mark each machine as a friend's or a stranger's. A friend's machine takes your jobs and the keys you grant. A stranger's runs only the sandboxes you send it, and never gets a key.
- **Share the Mac you already own.** Stop paying by the minute for macOS GitHub Actions jobs. Lend your Mac's spare time to your team and friends. Apple's licence forbids selling Mac time, not lending a macOS VM to your team (that is the makers' reading of the licence; read it yourself before you lend). Linux VMs on a Mac aren't affected.

## Guides

- A self-hosted GitHub Actions runner with a fresh VM for every job: https://potluck.sh/github-actions-runner
- Tart, its licence, and what Potluck adds: https://potluck.sh/tart
- A sandbox for AI coding agents on machines you own: https://potluck.sh/agent-sandbox

## Who makes it

Jackson and Clay at Sengi make Potluck. Write to ops@sengi.run, or use the form on the page. Mezze, the agent and team layer that runs on Potluck, has its own site: https://mezze.sh. It is for a team running a brigade of coding agents, and is a separate product. Sengi also runs hosted GitHub Actions runners for $1 per 1,000 minutes, with 3,000 free minutes a month: https://sengi.run

# A sandbox for AI coding agents on machines you own

Updated 2026-11-18. https://potluck.sh/agent-sandbox

An agent that runs commands on your laptop can read your files, your keys and your network. A sandbox moves those
commands onto a machine that holds none of that, and throws the machine away afterwards. Potluck finds that machine
among the ones your team already has: the Mac mini left on at night, the Linux box under a desk.

## Set it up with your agent

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent on the machine you want to try. Every command in it is
from Potluck's quick start, and it stops to ask before anything that needs a password, a sign-in or deleting files.

```text
Set up Potluck (https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck) on this machine so I can try it alone. Read https://potluck.sh/llms-full.txt first. Then:
1. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh (if it says ~/.local/bin is not on PATH, run the line it prints).
2. Run `potluck doctor` and tell me what is missing. On a Mac that is usually Tart, Softnet and about 60 GB of free disk. Show me any sudo line it prints; do not run sudo yourself.
3. When doctor is clean: potluck create trial --via tunnel, then potluck host --reclaim-idle-s 0 (on a Mac the first run pulls about 27 GB).
4. potluck sandbox create, then potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a, then potluck sandbox rm <id>.
Stop and ask me before anything that needs a password, a sign-in or deleting files. If a command fails, show me its exact output.
```

## Four ways in

| You use | Potluck gives you |
| --- | --- |
| A terminal or a script | `potluck sandbox create`, `potluck sandbox exec <id> -- <command>`, `potluck sandbox rm <id>` |
| An MCP client (Claude Code, Codex, an IDE) | `potluck mcp`: sandbox tools over MCP |
| Claude Code sessions started from claude.ai | `potluck agent-runner claude`: Claude Code's self-hosted runner, one fresh sandbox per session |
| Code written for E2B | `potluck-e2b`: the E2B SDK, pointed at your own machines |

### The sandbox commands

```sh
potluck sandbox create --template agent   # a Linux sandbox with Node, Python, git, Claude Code and Codex
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- make test
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

`--template agent` takes the agent image, which a Linux machine in your pool must lend; without it you get the
machine's default image. `--ref HEAD` sends your checkout's current commit into the sandbox.

### MCP

Add Potluck to an MCP client's configuration:

```json
{"mcpServers":{"potluck":{"command":"potluck","args":["mcp"]}}}
```

The server offers only sandbox tools: create, execute, list, extend, stop, restart, delete, background processes,
and file reads and writes. With more than one pool, add `"--pool","<name>"` before `"mcp"`. Treat what comes
back from a sandbox as untrusted data. Read more in
[Give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp).

### Claude Code's self-hosted runner

Claude Code can run sessions started on claude.ai on your own machines through a self-hosted environment, which a
person makes in claude.ai's admin settings. Its key is the environment secret:

```sh
potluck agent-runner claude --secret-file <key-file> --image ghcr.io/sengirunners/potluck-box-agent
```

Each session gets a fresh sandbox, and a new one starts as each ends; `--count` keeps several going. The session can
read the key, and the sandbox's network reaches the internet, so rotate the key after any session you suspect
([docs/agent-runners.md](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/blob/main/docs/agent-runners.md)).

### The E2B SDK

`potluck-e2b` answers the calls the E2B Python and TypeScript SDKs make, so code written for E2B runs on your pool
with only its environment changed. It covers create, run a command, read and write files, list, set a timeout,
connect and kill. Read more in
[Use the E2B SDK on your own machines](/blog/use-the-e2b-sdk-on-your-own-machines).

## What the sandbox keeps away from the agent

- **Your machine and network.** On a machine you trust, a sandbox reaches the internet but never the machine itself
  (on Tart, apart from Softnet's DNS forwarder on the host) or its local network ([docs/network.md](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/blob/main/docs/network.md)).
- **Your keys.** A sandbox starts with none of your credentials; a key goes in only when you send it, as a file.
- **Leftovers.** Each sandbox starts from the same image and is deleted at its time limit or when you remove it.


## On a Mac

macOS sandboxes run in Tart VMs, two at a time at most, as Apple's licence allows
([what Tart is, its licence, and what Potluck adds](/tart)). On a Mac, `potluck sandbox create` and the MCP tools give an agent a macOS VM to work in; `--template agent` and
`potluck agent-runner` use Linux machines.

## Running more than one agent

To run several agents and keep track of them, [Mezze for teams of coding agents](https://mezze.sh/), a separate product from the same makers that runs on Potluck, adds mail between agents and people and work items whose claims expire.

Source: https://potluck.sh/github-actions-runner

# Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner with a fresh VM for every job

Updated 2026-11-19. https://potluck.sh/github-actions-runner

A self-hosted runner that lives on one machine for months collects state: caches, half-installed tools, files a
job left behind, and anything a bad dependency dropped there. Potluck gives every job a fresh machine instead, on
hardware your team already owns.

## How a job runs

1. One machine in your pool runs Potluck's runner broker. It is connected to GitHub through a GitHub App you create,
   and it watches the repositories you connect. With a public address it takes GitHub's webhooks and catches up by
   asking GitHub every 5 minutes; with none, it asks GitHub for queued jobs every 15 seconds.
2. A queued job whose `runs-on` names your pool's label (for a pool called `friends`: `runs-on: friends`, or
   `friends:<size>` for a size, with or without `self-hosted`) is the pool's. A job that names no OS goes to Linux,
   as on GitHub's own runners.
3. The broker registers a just-in-time runner for that one job and asks a pool machine for a fresh box of the right
   size. GitHub's runner starts inside the box, takes the job, and the box is ended when the job is done.

A box is a Tart VM on an Apple-silicon Mac, or a container under Kata (a lightweight VM) or gVisor on Linux. Nothing
from one job is left for the next. On a Mac lent by a person, a job ends when its owner touches the keyboard or
trackpad, and nothing new starts until the Mac has been idle for five minutes; `potluck host set drain` winds any
machine down.

## Which jobs it takes, and which it refuses

- Only repositories you connect: `potluck runners allow <owner/repo>`. A public repository needs `--public`, your
  yes to serve its own branches.
- Only runs started by people who can push: `push`, `pull_request` from the repository's own branches,
  `workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`, `merge_group`, `release` and `repository_dispatch`. Never `pull_request_target`,
  `workflow_run`, `issue_comment` and the like, which act on outsiders' input.
- Never a run from a fork, unless you turn on `allow_fork_prs` for a private repository.

A refused job never runs on your machines. It stays queued on GitHub, or, if GitHub hands it a runner made for
another job, the box stops it before its first step and it fails. A fork can edit `runs-on` in its own pull request, so the
label alone would not keep it off your machines; the broker's refusal is what does. To have forks' pull requests
run on GitHub's runner instead, use the `runs-on` that `potluck ci pr` writes (below).

## Move one job onto your Mac: `potluck ci pr`

`potluck ci pr <owner/repo>` changes one job's `runs-on` in a workflow and prepares the change as a pull request
for you to open. A job that says `runs-on: macos-15` becomes:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ fromJSON(github.event.pull_request && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository && '["macos-15"]' || '["self-hosted","macos","<pool label>"]') }}
```

As written, pull requests from forks ask for `macos-15`, GitHub's runner. Pushes, manual runs, schedules and pull
requests from the repository's own branches ask for your pool. Only that one value in the file changes
([docs/ci-pr.md](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/blob/main/docs/ci-pr.md)).

## Set it up

Start with a pool and a machine that shares itself with it (the [quick start](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck#quick-start)).
Then, on the pool's machine:

```sh
potluck runners setup <pool>        # writes the broker's settings and prints the GitHub App's creation page
potluck runners allow <owner/repo>  # connect a repository (add --public for a public one)
potluck ci pr <owner/repo>          # prepare the pull request that moves one job onto the pool
potluck ci doctor <owner/repo>      # 17 read-only checks, each failure with one next step
```

Creating the GitHub App and linking its installation need a public https address that GitHub can send your browser
back to (for example a tunnel). Serving jobs afterwards does not need it: with no public address the broker asks GitHub itself, every 15 seconds. The details are in
[docs/daemon.md](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/blob/main/docs/daemon.md#github-runner-broker) and
[docs/ci-doctor.md](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/blob/main/docs/ci-doctor.md).

## What it costs

Potluck is free. GitHub does not charge for minutes on self-hosted runners; its billing docs list self-hosted runners
as free (read November 17, 2026). On a private repository, after your plan's included minutes, GitHub's standard
macOS runner costs $0.062 a minute and its 2-core Linux runner $0.006 a minute (GitHub's runner price list, read
November 17, 2026). On your own machines you pay for the electricity. For Linux jobs no machine of yours is free to
take, Sengi, the company that makes Potluck, runs [hosted Linux runners for GitHub Actions](https://sengi.run/alternatives/github-hosted-runners).

The machine that runs a job's VM can read everything in it, secrets included, so lend and use machines only among
people you trust with that.

On a Mac, Potluck uses Tart: [what Tart is and what Potluck adds](/tart).

---

Source: https://potluck.sh/tart

# Tart VMs for CI and agents: what Tart does, its licence, and what Potluck adds

Updated 2026-11-17. https://potluck.sh/tart

## What Tart does

Tart's README describes it as a virtualization toolset to build, run and manage macOS and Linux virtual machines on
Apple silicon, built by CI engineers for automation. It uses Apple's own Virtualization framework, so VMs run at close
to native speed. VM images are pushed to and pulled from any OCI-compatible container registry, the same kind of
registry that holds Docker images, and a Packer plugin builds them. Its site is [tart.run](https://tart.run).

Tart was started at Cirrus Labs. Its repository is now [github.com/openai/tart](https://github.com/openai/tart)
(the old cirruslabs/tart address leads there), and its licence names OpenAI as the copyright holder.

## Tart's licence: FSL-1.1-ALv2

Tart's LICENSE file is the Functional Source License, version 1.1, with Apache 2.0 as its future licence
(FSL-1.1-ALv2). In short:

- You may use, copy, change and redistribute Tart for any purpose except a "Competing Use", which the licence defines
  as "making the Software available to others in a commercial product or service that: 1. substitutes for the
  Software; 2. substitutes for any other product or service we offer using the Software that exists as of the date
  we make the Software available; or 3. offers the same or substantially similar functionality as the Software".
- The licence names internal use, non-commercial education and research, and professional services to someone who
  holds a licence as permitted.
- Each version becomes available under Apache 2.0 two years after it is made available.

Running Tart inside your own team to test your own code is internal use. Whether a particular business counts as a
Competing Use is a question for the licence text and your lawyer, not this page.

## Apple's limit: two macOS VMs per Mac

Apple's software licence agreement for macOS (section 2B(iii), in the copy shipped with macOS 27.2.1) allows up to
two additional copies or instances of macOS in virtual machines on each Apple-branded computer you own or control,
for software development, testing during software development, macOS Server, or personal non-commercial use. The
same agreement does not allow those VMs to be used for service-bureau, time-sharing, terminal-sharing or relay
services. Linux VMs on a Mac are not affected.

Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Its rule for lending: a macOS VM for people on your team or friends you
invite is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time
([the README's Macs section](https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck#macs)). That is Potluck's makers' reading of
the licence.

## Potluck does not bundle Tart

Potluck's installer puts `potluck`, its drivers, `potluck-conformance` and `potluck-e2b` on your machine, and nothing
else. On a Mac, you install Tart and Softnet (the helper Tart uses to give a VM an isolated network; it is setuid
root) yourself, and accept Tart's licence yourself. `potluck doctor` says what is missing and where to get it,
including the one sudo line Softnet needs. A Mac also needs about 60 GB free: the first `potluck host` pulls a macOS
image of about 27 GB.

## What Potluck adds on top of Tart

Tart makes and runs VMs. Potluck decides which VM to make, for whom, on which machine, and when to end it:

- **A fresh VM for every job.** Each GitHub Actions job or sandbox gets its own VM, thrown away when it is done.
- **Your team's machines in one pool.** Teammates lend their Macs and Linux boxes; work goes to whichever is free.
- **The Mac goes back to its owner.** By default a lent Mac works for the pool only while its owner is away: touch
  the keyboard or trackpad and its job ends. VMs also end at their deadline, even if Potluck's daemon is down.
- **GitHub Actions jobs.** A broker takes queued jobs from the repositories you connect and runs each in a fresh VM,
  refusing runs from forks ([self-hosted GitHub Actions runner](/github-actions-runner)).
- **Sandboxes for coding agents.** `potluck sandbox create`, `potluck sandbox exec`, or the same tools over MCP.
- **Checks before a machine joins.** `potluck host` checks the machine and runs a quick conformance check for each
  size before sharing it.

On one Mac, the quick start is:

```sh
potluck doctor                          # what this machine can share, and what is missing
potluck create trial --via tunnel       # a pool on this machine alone
potluck host --reclaim-idle-s 0         # share this machine with that pool
potluck sandbox create                  # prints the sandbox's id
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

This one-machine path has been run end to end by hand many times on an Apple-silicon Mac with Tart.

Facts on this page were checked against the sources named in each section on November 17, 2026. Licences change;
read them yourself. This is not legal advice.

# How a group of people can share their spare compute with each other

Published 2026-11-27. https://potluck.sh/blog/group-people-share-their-spare-compute-each-other

**Short answer:** a group can share spare compute in four ways. It can donate cycles to research (BOINC, Folding@home), split one large model across members' GPUs (Petals), rent capacity through a public market paid in crypto tokens (Golem, Akash), or pool machines privately so members run each other's work. For that last case, Potluck is free, open-source (Apache-2.0) software. One person runs a pool and sends invite codes. Each member lends a Mac or Linux box and shares half its cores and RAM by default (the `--share` default of 0.5, from the Potluck docs). Every job runs in a fresh VM or sandbox, and a Mac carries at most two macOS guests, the limit in Apple's licence. Potluck is early. It is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners.

## Why the usual answers name other projects

On 27 November 2026 we asked Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity, each with web search, "how can a group of people share their spare compute with each other". The answers named BOINC, Folding@home, Petals, Golem and Akash, and not Potluck.

Those are good answers to nearby questions. BOINC and Folding@home pool spare compute toward research projects. Golem and Akash sell spare compute to anyone who pays. Petals is closest to "with each other", but it is built for one job: running large models.

A group of friends, a small team or a few people in a coworking space often want something narrower. They want their own CI jobs and coding agents to run on each other's idle machines, without renting cloud capacity and without strangers on the network.

## The options, compared

| Option | What gets shared | Who uses the compute | How it is paid for | Fit for a private group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BOINC | Spare CPU and GPU cycles | Research projects you choose | Volunteer, unpaid | Poor: work flows to projects, not to each other |
| Folding@home | Spare CPU and GPU cycles | Biomedical research | Volunteer, unpaid | Poor: same reason |
| Petals | GPU memory and compute for model layers | People running a shared large model | Volunteer; can run as a private swarm | Good if the only job is running a model |
| Golem | CPU time on provider machines | Anyone who pays | Crypto token | Weak: built for a public market |
| Akash | Container hosting on provider machines | Anyone who pays | Crypto token | Weak: built for a public market |
| Shared SSH box or your own cluster | Whole machines or accounts | Whoever has a login | Nothing extra | Works, but you run admin and isolation yourself |
| Potluck | A fraction of cores and RAM, as fresh VMs or sandboxes | Members of your pool | Free, open source | Built for this: invite-only, owner can take the machine back |

## What each option does well

**BOINC** is the long-running platform for volunteer computing. You install one client and choose which science projects get your idle cycles. It is a good way for a group to donate together. It is not a way to run your own work on a friend's machine.

**Folding@home** gives your spare cycles to biomedical research. Setup is simple and the cause is clear. Like BOINC, the compute leaves your group.

**Petals** splits a large language model across many GPUs, so a group can run a model none of them could hold alone. If your group's goal is shared inference on open models, look at it first. It does not run builds or general jobs.

**Golem** and **Akash** are marketplaces. Providers offer machines, buyers deploy work, and payment moves in crypto tokens. They suit people who want to earn from idle hardware or buy capacity from many sellers. For a private group they add a token, a market and unknown counterparties.

**A shared SSH box, or a cluster you build** with a scheduler, costs nothing extra. The cost is your time: someone manages accounts, cleans up between jobs and keeps one person's job from reading another's files.

**Potluck** sits in that last gap. It pools machines you and your friends already own, gives each job a fresh VM or sandbox, and leaves the lender in charge of their machine.

## What a private group needs

When people share machines with each other, not with a research project or a market, four things matter.

1. **Invite-only membership.** Only people you invite can send work or lend machines.
2. **A clean box per job.** One member's build should not see the leftovers of another's.
3. **The owner comes first.** If you sit down at your Mac, you want it back now.
4. **Clear trust lines.** You should know who can read what.

## How Potluck shares compute inside a group

One person runs the pool. On that machine, `potluck create friends` makes a pool called friends. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL, because machines in a pool reach each other over Tailscale or over a tunnel you configure.

The pool owner then hands out codes:

- `potluck invite ana` makes a code for Ana, who will run sandboxes on the pool.
- `potluck invite carl --host` makes a code for Carl, who will share a machine.

Ana runs `potluck join '<code>'`. Carl runs `potluck host '<code>'`. Before Carl's machine joins, `potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image and runs a quick conformance check for each size. The machine joins the pool only when a size passes.

Carl decides how much to lend with `--share`. The default of 0.5 means half his cores and RAM. When he wants the machine back, `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

What runs on a lent machine depends on the machine:

- **Apple silicon Mac:** macOS VMs through Tart. A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer.
- **Linux box:** containers through Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor.

When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. Hand-back when the owner returns works on a Mac. On Linux it works only as a time window today.

For coding agents, `potluck --pool friends mcp` runs an MCP server that gives an agent sandbox tools. See [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) and the [agent sandbox page](/agent-sandbox). `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.

For CI, Potluck has run a real GitHub Actions job through its runner broker, by hand, in two setups: on a Mac with Tart, and on a Linux box on another machine with gVisor. It does not yet run daily in our own CI. The [GitHub Actions runner page](/github-actions-runner) covers that work.

## What to trust, and what not to

Sharing compute among people means trusting people, and software cannot remove that.

- The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets.
- The machine that runs a pool can read the commands and output that pass through it.

So join only a pool whose owner you trust, and lend only to people you would hand a laptop to. Potluck comes with no promises; use it at your own risk.

What Potluck can check is the other direction: keeping the job away from the lender's network. `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On the OCI layer the default is no network at all. For how these isolation layers differ, see the [coding agent sandboxing guide](/blog/coding-agent-sandboxing-guide-containers-gvisor-vms-compared).

## Rules for sharing Macs

Macs carry licence limits that Linux boxes do not.

- Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac.
- Lending a macOS guest to your team or to invited friends is fine.
- Selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time.

This is not legal advice. More on Mac setups is on the [Tart page](/tart) and in [giving coding agents their own Mac](/blog/giving-coding-agents-their-own-mac-macos-vms).

## What Potluck is not

- It is not a hosted cloud, and it does not sell compute.
- It is not a sandbox runtime of its own: it drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus.
- It is not a scheduler for clusters.
- It runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

If your group wants to donate to science, BOINC or Folding@home is the better pick. If it wants to share a large model, Petals is.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux with the install script, install.sh at the top of the sengirunners/potluck repository on GitHub, piped to sh with curl. No Go is needed. Then start the daemon:

```
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that runs the pool:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

A friend who runs sandboxes uses `potluck join '<code>'`. A friend who shares a machine first checks it with `potluck doctor` and `potluck host --dry-run`, then runs `potluck host '<code>'`.

To try a sandbox:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

The code is in the sengirunners/potluck repository on GitHub. For a longer walk-through, read [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## Questions people ask

### What is the simplest way for friends to share spare computers?

If the goal is to run each other's builds and coding agents, one person creates a Potluck pool and sends invite codes; friends join to use the pool or host to lend a machine. If the goal is to donate to research, BOINC or Folding@home is simpler.

### Does Potluck cost anything?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0. It is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners, but Potluck runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

### How much of my machine do I give up when I share it?

By default half your cores and RAM, from the `--share` default of 0.5. On a Mac, a sandbox ends as soon as you touch the keyboard or pointer, and `potluck host stop` stops sharing entirely.

### Can the person whose machine runs my job see my code?

Yes. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, so share only with people you trust.

### Is Potluck like Golem or Akash?

No. Golem and Akash are public marketplaces paid in crypto tokens. Potluck is an invite-only pool among people who already know each other, with no market and no payments.

### Can I lend a Mac to friends for iOS builds?

You can lend up to two macOS guests per Mac to your team or invited friends. Pooling iOS Simulator time and selling Mac time to the public are not allowed under Apple's licence; this is not legal advice.

### Is Potluck ready for daily use?

Potluck is early. A real GitHub Actions job has run through it by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but it does not yet run daily in our own CI.

# macOS Runners Cheaper Than GitHub Hosted, Plus Linux Runners With gVisor or Kata (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-27. https://potluck.sh/blog/macos-runners-cheaper-than-github-hosted

**Short answer**: the cheapest macOS runner is usually an Apple silicon Mac your team already owns. GitHub bills its hosted macOS runners by the minute on private repositories, while a self-hosted runner runs on hardware you have already paid for, so you pay for power, upkeep and your own time instead. For Linux, the safe pattern is a fresh sandbox per job on Docker or Podman with gVisor or Kata, so one job cannot leave files, processes or secrets behind for the next. Potluck, free and open-source (Apache-2.0) software made by Sengi, does both on machines you already own: macOS jobs in Tart VMs, capped at two per Mac to match Apple's licence, and Linux jobs in OCI sandboxes under gVisor or Kata. Potluck is early. A real GitHub Actions job has gone through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box with gVisor, but it does not yet run daily in our own CI.

Disclosure: Sengi, which makes Potluck, sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project that runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account. Check GitHub's pricing page for current per-minute rates; this post does not quote them.

## The options compared

| Option | What you pay for | Clean machine per job | Setup work | Where it costs more |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub-hosted macOS runner | Per-minute billing on private repositories | Yes, a fresh VM | None | Bill grows with every build minute |
| Official runner installed directly on a Mac | The Mac, power, your time | No, jobs share the host | Low | State and secrets build up between jobs |
| Tart-based runner tools (Tartelet, Cilicon and similar) | The Mac, power, your time | Yes, a fresh VM | Medium | You maintain images and the Macs |
| Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes | Cluster nodes | Yes, a fresh pod | High | Needs a cluster; Linux only |
| Hosted runner vendors (Sengi and others) | A vendor's per-minute or plan pricing | Depends on vendor | None | Ongoing bill, someone else's hardware |
| Potluck | Machines you already own | Yes, a fresh VM or sandbox | Medium | Early; Actions broker tested by hand, not yet daily |

GitHub-hosted runners are the easiest choice: nothing to buy, a clean VM every time, and GitHub keeps the images current. Hosted vendors offer the same convenience with different hardware and pricing. The self-hosted rows trade that convenience for a lower running cost. For more detail on each, see [best self-hosted CI runners](/blog/best-self-hosted-ci-runners), [Tart-based runners compared](/blog/tart-based-github-actions-runners-compared-tartelet-cilicon) and [Actions Runner Controller](/blog/actions-runner-controller-github-actions-runner-controller-arc).

## Why a Mac you own is cheaper than a hosted macOS runner

A hosted macOS runner charges for every minute a job runs. A Mac on a desk is already paid for, and most team Macs sit idle at night, at weekends and during meetings. The extra cost of running builds on it is mostly electricity and the time someone spends keeping it working.

That time is real, and it is where self-hosting costs more:

- **Images.** You keep macOS and Xcode versions current yourself. GitHub does this for you on hosted runners.
- **Clean state.** The official runner installed straight on a Mac reuses the same user account for every job. Caches, keychains and leftover files carry over. A fresh VM per job fixes this, which is what Tart-based tools and Potluck do. See [self-hosted macOS runners with a fresh VM every job](/blog/self-hosted-macos-runners-fresh-vm-every-job).
- **Availability.** A laptop leaves the office. A desktop owner wants their machine back. Your builds have to cope.
- **Hardware failure.** When a disk dies, nobody else replaces it.

There is also a licence limit. Apple's macOS licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending those guests to your team or to invited friends fits the licence; selling Mac time to the public does not, and neither does pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

One more cost to watch: in December 2025 GitHub announced a per-minute platform charge for self-hosted runner usage on private repositories, then postponed it within a day, as Winbuzzer reported at the time. Check GitHub's billing documentation for the current state before you budget.

## How to run self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on a Linux box with gVisor or Kata

A plain Docker container shares the host's kernel. If a job escapes the container, or a malicious pull request runs code you did not expect, it is running on your box. gVisor puts a user-space kernel between the job and the host kernel. Kata runs each container inside a lightweight VM. Both plug into Docker or Podman as a container runtime, so the workflow stays the same.

The pattern, with or without Potluck:

1. Install Docker or Podman on the Linux box.
2. Install gVisor or Kata and register it as a runtime, following each project's own documentation.
3. Run each job in a new container under that runtime, and register the GitHub runner in ephemeral mode so it takes one job and exits.
4. Delete the container after the job, and start the next job from the clean image.
5. Cut the sandbox off from the host, your LAN and anything else you would not hand to a stranger.

Step 5 is the one people skip. With Potluck, `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet, and on the OCI layer the default is no network at all. Before a Linux box joins a pool, `potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image and runs a quick conformance check for each sandbox size; the box joins only when a size passes. `potluck doctor` shows what the machine can share, and `potluck host --dry-run` prints the plan.

One Linux limit today: Potluck hands a Linux box back to its owner only as a time window. On a Mac, a sandbox ends when the owner touches the keyboard or pointer.

For how gVisor, Kata, containers and full VMs compare as isolation, read [the coding agent sandboxing guide](/blog/coding-agent-sandboxing-guide-containers-gvisor-vms-compared).

## What Potluck does today, and what it does not

What exists:

- A `potluck` program (the daemon and the commands), signed releases for macOS and Linux, and an install script.
- Pools: one machine runs the pool, friends join to run sandboxes, and other friends share their machines. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure.
- Sharing on an Apple silicon Mac with Tart, or on Linux with Docker or Podman plus Kata or gVisor.
- A runner broker for GitHub Actions. A real Actions job has been run through it by hand on a Mac (Tart) and on a Linux box on another machine (OCI with gVisor).
- `potluck agent-runner`, which runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.

What it is not yet: the Actions path is not running daily in our own CI. Potluck is also not a hosted cloud, not a sandbox runtime of its own (it drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus) and not a scheduler for clusters. If you need a cluster scheduler, Actions Runner Controller is built for that. More on the runner side at [GitHub Actions runner](/github-actions-runner) and [Tart](/tart).

## Trust: who can see your jobs

Self-hosting moves trust onto people and machines you pick. With Potluck:

- The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets.
- The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it.
- Join only a pool whose owner you trust.

Use it at your own risk; there are no promises. For a team pooling its own desks, this usually matches how trust already works. For public repositories that accept outside pull requests, think hard about which secrets a job can see.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux with the one-line install script from the sengirunners/potluck repository on GitHub (the file is install.sh; download it with curl and pipe it to sh, no Go needed). Then start the daemon:

```
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that will run the pool:

```
potluck create friends
```

The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL. Then make invite codes:

```
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

`ana` gets a code to run sandboxes; `carl` gets a code to share a machine. On Carl's Mac or Linux box:

```
potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'
```

The `--share` flag sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared; the default is 0.5. `potluck host stop` stops sharing. Ana joins with `potluck join '<code>'` and tries a sandbox:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

To give a coding agent the same sandboxes, `potluck --pool friends mcp` runs an MCP server with sandbox tools. The code lives in the sengirunners/potluck repository on GitHub. For a longer walkthrough, see [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## Questions people ask

### Are self-hosted macOS runners cheaper than GitHub-hosted ones?

Usually, if you already own the Macs and they sit idle. You stop paying per minute and start paying in upkeep time: images, Xcode versions and hardware.

### How many macOS VMs can I run on one Mac?

Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. This is not legal advice.

### Can I sell spare Mac build time with Potluck?

No. Lending macOS guests to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time.

### Should I use gVisor or Kata for Linux runners?

Both work with Docker or Podman, and Potluck can share a Linux box with either. gVisor adds a user-space kernel in front of the host kernel, while Kata runs each container in a lightweight VM; run `potluck doctor` to see what your box can share.

### Is Potluck ready to replace my GitHub-hosted runners?

Not yet. It is early: a real Actions job has run through the runner broker by hand on a Mac and on Linux with gVisor, but it is not yet in daily use in our own CI.

### Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account; Sengi, which makes it, sells hosted runners as a separate product.

### What happens if a Mac owner sits down mid-build?

The Mac sandbox ends when the owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused.

# Actions Runner Controller (ARC): Self-Hosted GitHub Actions Runners on Kubernetes in 2026

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/actions-runner-controller-github-actions-runner-controller-arc

**Short answer**: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) is the Kubernetes operator from the actions/actions-runner-controller repository that runs and autoscales self-hosted GitHub Actions runners as ephemeral pods. The GitHub Docs page "Actions Runner Controller" says ARC ships as 2 Helm charts and 1 controller container image. You run 2 `helm install` commands: one for the gha-runner-scale-set-controller chart, and one gha-runner-scale-set chart per runner scale set. Then you set `runs-on` to the installation name, which the same page limits to 45 characters. Per that page, a failed runner pod is retried up to 5 times, and GitHub unassigns a job that no runner accepts within 24 hours. ARC needs a Kubernetes cluster and runs Linux container pods. If your spare capacity is Macs and Linux boxes rather than a cluster, Potluck, an early open-source project, runs jobs in a fresh VM or sandbox on machines you already own.

The rest of this page is a setup reference. Each fact names the GitHub Docs page or repository it comes from. The last part shows where Potluck fits.

## What Actions Runner Controller (ARC) is

The repository description calls actions-runner-controller a "Kubernetes controller for GitHub Actions self-hosted runners". The GitHub Docs concept page describes it as an operator that orchestrates and scales those runners.

- **Runner scale sets are the supported mode.** The repository README says the older autoscaling modes are legacy and maintained by the community only.
- **Charts are OCI only.** The concept page says the charts are published as OCI packages on GitHub Packages. There are no tarballs and no Helm repository on GitHub Pages.
- **ARC adds custom resources.** The concept page lists the API groups `actions.github.com/v1alpha1` (scale sets) and `actions.summerwind.net/v1alpha1` (legacy). The controller chart installs them.

## ARC compared with other runner options

Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate, free project.

| Option | Where jobs run | What you operate | macOS jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| ARC runner scale sets | Pods in your Kubernetes cluster | The cluster, 2 Helm releases, GitHub auth, logs | No, Linux container pods |
| One self-hosted runner | A machine you own | The runner app, cleanup between jobs | Yes, on a Mac |
| Hosted runners (GitHub-hosted, Cirrus Runners, Blacksmith, Sengi) | The vendor's machines | Nothing; the vendor bills you | Where the vendor offers it |
| Potluck | A fresh VM or sandbox on Macs and Linux boxes you own | A `potluck` daemon per machine, Tailscale or your own tunnel | Yes, with Tart on Apple silicon |

ARC is GitHub-supported and autoscales with workflow demand. A single runner is the simplest option, but it has no autoscaling and does not give each job a clean environment. Hosted runners need no hardware. Potluck is early: its Actions path has been run by hand, not yet daily.

## Prerequisites for ARC on Kubernetes

The GitHub Docs tutorial "Get started with Actions Runner Controller" lists:

- A Kubernetes cluster. It suggests a managed service such as AKS, or minikube or kind for a local trial.
- Helm 3.
- A way to collect and keep logs from the controller, listeners and ephemeral runners before production. The tutorial recommends this but does not require it.

## Step 1: install the gha-runner-scale-set-controller chart

This step installs the operator and the CRDs. The commands come from the quickstart:

```bash
NAMESPACE="arc-systems"
helm install arc \
  --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" \
  --create-namespace \
  oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set-controller
```

Once you move past a trial, pin a chart version with `--version`. The namespace must be able to reach the Kubernetes API server.

## Step 2: authenticate ARC to the GitHub API

The docs page "Authenticating ARC to the GitHub API" covers authentication.

- For repository or organization runners, GitHub recommends a GitHub App.
- Enterprise-level scale sets require a personal access token (classic).
- The quickstart uses a classic token with the `repo` and `admin:org` scopes to keep the trial short.

The quickstart warns against passing secrets in plain text on the command line. Create a Kubernetes secret instead:

```bash
kubectl create namespace arc-runners
kubectl create secret generic arc-github-secret \
  --namespace arc-runners \
  --from-literal=github_token='<PAT>'
```

## Step 3: deploy a runner scale set

The installation name becomes your `runs-on` value. The quickstart recommends keeping runner pods in a different namespace from the controller.

```bash
INSTALLATION_NAME="arc-runner-set"
NAMESPACE="arc-runners"
GITHUB_CONFIG_URL="<URL of your repository, organization or enterprise>"
helm install "${INSTALLATION_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" \
  --set githubConfigUrl="${GITHUB_CONFIG_URL}" \
  --set githubConfigSecret=arc-github-secret \
  oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set
```

The concept page's resource table says that when `githubConfigSecret` is a string, ARC uses that existing secret instead of creating one.

Resource names are the installation name plus a fixed suffix, so keep the name short. For example, the listener Role reserves 26 characters for its suffix.

To route jobs by other names, set `runnerScaleSetName` or `runnerScaleSetLabels` in `values.yaml`.

## Step 4: verify the install and run a workflow

```bash
helm list -A
kubectl get pods -n arc-systems
```

You should see both releases deployed, plus a controller pod and a listener pod in `Running`. Then add a workflow:

```yaml
name: Actions Runner Controller Demo
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  Explore-GitHub-Actions:
    runs-on: arc-runner-set
    steps:
      - run: echo "This job uses runner scale set runners"
```

Trigger it by hand and watch a runner pod come and go with `kubectl get pods -n arc-runners -w`. If a pod stays pending, see the GitHub Docs page "Troubleshooting Actions Runner Controller errors".

## How ARC scales runners

The architecture section of the concept page describes this flow:

1. The controller fetches the runner group and creates the scale set in the GitHub Actions service.
2. A listener pod holds an HTTPS long poll and waits for a Job Available message.
3. When a job's `runs-on` matches, the listener patches the EphemeralRunnerSet replica count.
4. The EphemeralRunner controller gets a just-in-time token and creates runner pods. It retries a failed pod up to 5 times.
5. When the job finishes, the runner is deleted.

Each job gets a new pod.

## Custom runner images

The concept page lists what GitHub's minimal runner image contains: runner binaries, container hooks, and Docker for Docker-in-Docker mode.

To add tools, use setup actions such as actions/setup-node, or build your own image. A custom image must:

- place the runner under `/home/runner/` and start it with `/home/runner/run.sh`;
- in Kubernetes mode, put the container hooks under `/home/runner/k8s`.

## Where Potluck fits

ARC assumes a Kubernetes cluster and Linux pods. Many teams that ask about running jobs on spare Macs have no cluster. They have a Mac mini on a shelf and a Linux box under a desk.

Potluck is free, Apache-2.0 software that runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on those machines, each in a fresh VM or sandbox.

- **Runtimes:** Tart on Apple silicon, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux.
- **Not a cluster scheduler:** if you already run Kubernetes, ARC is the better fit for Linux jobs.
- **Status:** a real Actions job has been run through the runner broker by hand, on a Mac (Tart) and on a Linux box on another machine (OCI with gVisor). It does not run daily in our own CI yet.
- **Coding agents:** `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.
- **Owners come first:** a Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
- **macOS limit:** Apple's licence allows 2 macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at 2 per Mac.

More: [GitHub Actions runners on your own machines](/github-actions-runner), [a self-hosted runner on your Mac](/blog/self-hosted-github-actions-runner-on-your-mac), [pooling spare Macs and Linux boxes](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## How to start with Potluck

Install and start the daemon on macOS or Linux (no Go needed):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

Set up a pool:

1. On the pool machine, run `potluck create friends`. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL.
2. Run `potluck invite ana` to make a code for a friend who runs sandboxes.
3. Run `potluck invite carl --host` to make a code for a friend who shares a machine.
4. Friends run `potluck join '<code>'` or `potluck host '<code>'`.

Before you share a machine:

- `potluck doctor` shows what the machine can share.
- `potluck host --dry-run` prints the plan.
- `--share` sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared (default 0.5).
- `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

Try a sandbox with `potluck sandbox create`, `potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a` and `potluck sandbox rm <id>`. To stop sharing, run `potluck host stop`.

Trust works like this. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The pool machine can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use Potluck at your own risk.

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. Contributors can find good first issues at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### What is Actions Runner Controller (ARC)?

ARC is a Kubernetes operator that runs and autoscales self-hosted GitHub Actions runners as ephemeral pods. It lives in the actions/actions-runner-controller repository, and its documentation is on GitHub Docs.

### Is ARC supported by GitHub?

The runner scale set mode is supported by GitHub. The README says the legacy autoscaling modes are maintained by the community only.

### Should ARC use a GitHub App or a personal access token?

GitHub Docs recommends a GitHub App for repository and organization runners. Enterprise-level scale sets require a personal access token (classic).

### Can ARC run macOS jobs?

No. ARC runners are Linux container pods. For macOS jobs you need a Mac, a hosted macOS runner, or a Tart VM through Potluck on Apple silicon.

### Does Potluck replace ARC?

No. Potluck is not a cluster scheduler. It puts idle Macs and Linux boxes to work in fresh VMs or sandboxes.

### Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

# Open Source Self-Hosted CI Runner Tools for CI Jobs and Coding Agents on Your Own Machines (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/best-self-hosted-ci-runners

**Short answer**: in November 2026 there are eight open-source tools worth a look for running CI jobs, and in one case coding agents, on hardware you already own. They are the GitHub Actions runner with actions-runner-controller, GitLab Runner, the Buildkite Agent, Jenkins with agent clouds, Woodpecker CI, Tekton, Concourse and Potluck. The first seven are CI systems or CI agents that run jobs on Linux servers or a Kubernetes cluster you operate. Potluck is different: it pools a team's idle Macs and Linux boxes, runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding-agent sandboxes there, and gives every job a fresh VM or sandbox. Potluck is free, Apache-2.0 licensed and early. Disclosure: Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners; Potluck is a separate free project and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account.

The tools differ less in what they can build than in what separates one job from the next. Pick on that first, then on what you already run.

## The options side by side

| Tool | What it runs | What separates jobs | Where it fits | Where it costs more work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions runner + actions-runner-controller | GitHub Actions jobs | A pod per job on Kubernetes, shared node kernel unless you add Kata or gVisor | GitHub teams already running Kubernetes | You need a cluster; GitHub's own docs warn against self-hosted runners on public repos |
| GitLab Runner | GitLab CI jobs | Depends on the executor: shell (none), docker (container), kubernetes (pod), instance executors (VM) | GitLab teams who choose the executor on purpose | The executor line is easy to set once and forget |
| Buildkite Agent | Buildkite pipelines | A host process by default; containers through plugins or hooks | Teams that want hosted coordination with all compute on their side | Coordination is a Buildkite service; isolation is yours to build |
| Jenkins with agent clouds | Jenkins pipelines | A pod, container or instance per build, by cloud plugin | Existing Jenkins installs with plugins nothing else has | Controller and plugin upkeep; agent images go stale |
| Woodpecker CI | Container pipelines | A container per step | Small setups, homelabs, Gitea or Forgejo | Smaller ecosystem; privileged steps for image builds |
| Tekton | Kubernetes-native pipelines | A pod per run | Platform teams building CI as an internal product | Verbose; most teams add a layer on top |
| Concourse | Resource-and-job pipelines | A container per step with declared inputs and outputs | Teams that want reproducible builds enforced by the tool | An unfamiliar model and its own ecosystem |
| Potluck | GitHub Actions jobs and coding-agent sandboxes | A fresh Tart VM on Apple silicon, or a Kata or gVisor sandbox on Linux | Teams with spare Macs and Linux boxes, including macOS work | Early; Linux hand-back is only a time window today |

## The CI runners, one by one

### GitHub Actions runner with actions-runner-controller

If your code is on GitHub and you run Kubernetes, this is the default. The runner is GitHub's own agent, and actions-runner-controller scales it as ephemeral runners that take one job and go away. You get a reset filesystem per job and autoscaling on queue depth. The boundary is a pod, so concurrent jobs on a node share a kernel. GitHub's documentation warns against self-hosted runners on public repositories, because a fork pull request can run code on your runner. If you build forks, put a VM-backed runtime under the pods or run those jobs elsewhere.

### GitLab Runner

GitLab Runner is one binary with several executors, and the executor is your isolation model. The shell executor runs jobs on the host in a reused build directory. The docker executor gives a fresh container per job. The kubernetes executor gives a pod per job. Instance executors give a VM per job at the cost of provisioning time. All are reasonable for the right repo; the risk is picking one from a setup prompt and never revisiting it, or adding privileged mode or a mounted Docker socket to make image builds work.

### Buildkite Agent

Buildkite splits the work: pipelines, scheduling and the UI are a hosted service, and the open-source agent runs on your machines. Source, secrets and artifacts stay on your side. This suits fleets spread across data centres and clouds. By default the agent runs jobs as host processes, so containers or VMs are something you set up through plugins or hooks.

### Jenkins with agent clouds

Jenkins still has a huge installed base. With a Kubernetes, Docker or cloud plugin it creates an agent per build and tears it down after. The work is in keeping agent images fresh, patching plugins and keeping builds off the controller, which holds credentials for everything it builds.

### Woodpecker CI

Woodpecker, a community fork of Drone, is a small server plus agents where every pipeline step is a container. Setup is short and one person can hold the whole thing in their head. It fits trusted code on small fleets, often next to a self-hosted Gitea or Forgejo.

### Tekton

Tekton models CI as Kubernetes resources: Tasks, Pipelines, PipelineRuns. You get the cluster's RBAC, GitOps and monitoring for free. A simple build takes more YAML than in other tools, so teams usually put a generator or dashboard in front.

### Concourse

Concourse runs every step in a container with declared inputs and outputs and no ambient state. Builds come out reproducible by design. Migrating an existing pipeline means modelling it properly, which takes time.

## What about coding agents?

The seven CI tools above run pipelines. A coding agent needs something else: a place to run commands, install packages and run tests that is not your laptop, created on demand and thrown away after. You can build that yourself with containers plus Kata or gVisor, or with VMs, and wire it to the agent. That works and is a fair amount of glue.

Potluck covers two agent cases on machines you own. `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes. `potluck --pool friends mcp` is an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent, so the agent can create a sandbox, run commands in it and remove it. More on that in [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) and [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines), or the [agent sandbox page](/agent-sandbox).

## Where Potluck fits, and where it does not

Potluck is not a hosted cloud, not a sandbox runtime of its own and not a scheduler for clusters. It drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus. What it adds is the pool: one machine runs it, friends join or share machines, and machines reach each other over Tailscale or a tunnel you configure.

What works today, from the Potluck facts:

- A real GitHub Actions job has been run through the runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine with OCI and gVisor. It is not yet running daily in Potluck's own CI. See the [GitHub Actions runner page](/github-actions-runner).
- Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux.
- `potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes.
- On the OCI layer the default is no network at all, and `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.
- A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.

If you already run Kubernetes and actions-runner-controller or GitLab Runner covers your needs, keep it. Potluck is for the case where the spare capacity is a few desks of Macs and Linux boxes, not a cluster.

## macOS jobs on a Mac you own

The GitHub, GitLab and Buildkite agents all have macOS builds, but on a bare Mac they run jobs on the host, so one job can leave state for the next. A VM per job fixes that. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice. Details in [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac](/blog/self-hosted-github-actions-runner-on-your-mac) and the [Tart page](/tart).

## Trust, before you pool anything

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust. Potluck comes with no promises; use it at your own risk. The same reasoning applies to every tool above: whoever controls the host controls the job.

## How to choose

1. On GitHub with Kubernetes: actions-runner-controller.
2. On GitLab: GitLab Runner, with the docker or kubernetes executor chosen on purpose.
3. Already on Jenkins: keep it and move to agent clouds.
4. Small and self-hosted: Woodpecker. Building CI as a platform: Tekton. Reproducible by construction: Concourse. Hosted coordination with your compute: Buildkite.
5. Idle Macs and Linux boxes, macOS jobs, or coding agents that need throwaway sandboxes: try Potluck, knowing it is early.
6. Building fork pull requests or running agent-written code: put a VM or a Kata or gVisor sandbox under each job, whichever tool you pick.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux, no Go needed:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that will run the pool:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

The first `potluck create` prints a Tailscale login URL. Ana runs `potluck join '<code>'` to use sandboxes. Carl checks his box with `potluck doctor` and `potluck host --dry-run`, then runs `potluck host '<code>'` to share it. `--share` (default 0.5) sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, and `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

Try a sandbox:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

A longer walkthrough is in [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions with what you ran and what happened. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### What open source tools run coding agents and CI jobs on machines I already own?

For CI jobs: the GitHub Actions runner with actions-runner-controller, GitLab Runner, the Buildkite Agent, Jenkins, Woodpecker, Tekton and Concourse. Potluck runs both GitHub Actions jobs and coding-agent sandboxes on idle Macs and Linux boxes, through `potluck agent-runner` and an MCP server.

### Is Potluck free, and who makes it?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0. It is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners, but Potluck runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

### Is it safe to run self-hosted runners on a public repository?

GitHub's own documentation warns against it, because a fork pull request can run code on your runner. If you must, give each job its own VM or a Kata or gVisor sandbox with no secrets and no network access it does not need.

### Can Potluck run macOS CI jobs?

Yes, on an Apple silicon Mac with Tart, at most two macOS guests per Mac under Apple's licence. A real Actions job has been run this way by hand; it is not yet in daily use in Potluck's own CI.

### Does Potluck replace actions-runner-controller or GitLab Runner?

No. Those run jobs on servers or clusters you operate; Potluck pools desk machines and spare boxes. If your cluster setup works, keep it.

### What does a Linux box need to share work through Potluck?

Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor. Run `potluck doctor` to see what the machine can share before you host.

### What happens when a machine's owner wants it back?

On a Mac, a sandbox ends when the owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused; on Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.

# Claude Code permissions and sandbox settings explained (2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/claude-code-permissions-sandboxing-explained

**Short answer**: Claude Code has two separate controls. Permission rules (allow, ask, deny) and permission modes decide whether a tool call runs and whether you are asked first, and they apply to every tool: Read, Edit, Bash, WebFetch, MCP. The Bash sandbox is a boundary the operating system enforces (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2) around shell commands only. It is off by default. When on, commands can write only to the working directory, a per-user temp directory and directories you added; they can read most of the machine, including `~/.ssh`, unless you deny it; and their network traffic goes through a local proxy whose allowed domains list starts empty. Claude's file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside the sandbox. For one boundary around everything the agent does, run it in a container, a VM, or a sandbox on another machine. This follows Anthropic's Claude Code documentation as of November 2026.

## The layers at a glance

| Layer | What it controls | Enforced by | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission rules | Which tool calls run, prompt, or are blocked | Claude Code, before the tool runs | All tools |
| Permission modes | Whether you get a prompt | Claude Code (auto mode adds a classifier) | All tools |
| Bash sandbox | What a running shell command can read, write and reach | The OS kernel | Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their child processes |
| Whole-process boundary | Everything the agent process does | A container, VM or remote sandbox | The agent, its file tools, MCP servers and hooks |

The University of Vermont IT knowledge base names the most common mistake: assuming the sandbox restricts everything Claude reads. It does not. A sandbox `denyRead` entry does not stop the Read tool, and `allowedDomains` does not limit WebFetch. Block a secret in both places, or the other path still reaches it.

## Permission rules: allow, ask, deny

Rules live in `permissions` in a settings file and use patterns such as `Read(...)`, `Edit(...)`, `Bash(git push *)` and `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`. Per the UVM article, they are evaluated deny first, then ask, then allow, and a deny set in managed settings cannot be re-allowed by a user. Watch the path syntax: in Read and Edit rules, `//path` is absolute and `/path` is relative to the project, while sandbox filesystem settings use ordinary paths such as `/tmp/build` and `~/.kube`.

## Permission modes

Modes decide who approves a call. Manual mode prompts; acceptEdits approves file edits; auto mode hands the decision to a classifier model; dontAsk refuses anything not already allowed; plan mode gates commands while you plan; bypassPermissions (the `--dangerously-skip-permissions` flag) skips prompts. `/sandbox` is not a mode. The sandbox's own auto-allow setting approves Bash commands because the sandbox contains them, which is different from auto mode's classifier. You can combine the two.

## What the Bash sandbox restricts by default

| Access | Default when enabled | Change it with |
|---|---|---|
| Writes | Working directory, per-user temp directory, added directories; protected paths such as `.claude` settings, `.mcp.json` and `.bashrc` stay write-denied | `filesystem.allowWrite`, `filesystem.denyWrite` |
| Reads | Most of the machine, including credential files | `filesystem.denyRead`, `filesystem.allowRead`, `credentials` |
| Network | No direct route out; a proxy checks each host against an allowlist that starts empty | `network.allowedDomains`, `network.deniedDomains`, `network.strictAllowlist` |
| Environment | Inherited from Claude Code, secrets included | `credentials.envVars`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB` |

Turn it on with `/sandbox` in a session and pick auto-allow or regular permissions, or set `sandbox.enabled` to true in `~/.claude/settings.json`. On Linux and WSL2, install `bubblewrap` and `socat` first. To check it works, ask Claude (not the `!` prompt, which runs unsandboxed) to run `touch ~/sandbox-probe`; it should fail.

A starting point for user settings that blocks SSH and AWS keys, strips a token, allows two registries and stops unsandboxed retries:

```json
{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false,
    "failIfUnavailable": true,
    "network": { "allowedDomains": ["github.com", "*.npmjs.org"] },
    "credentials": {
      "files": [
        { "path": "~/.ssh", "mode": "deny" },
        { "path": "~/.aws/credentials", "mode": "deny" }
      ],
      "envVars": [ { "name": "GITHUB_TOKEN", "mode": "deny" } ]
    }
  }
}
```

There is no built-in credential deny list; only what you name is protected.

## The escape hatches

- **Unsandboxed retry**: after a failure Claude can retry with `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`. Setting `allowUnsandboxedCommands` to false (strict sandbox mode) removes it.
- **excludedCommands**: matching commands run with your full access. Docker does not work inside the sandbox, so `docker compose *` here is common; keep patterns narrow.
- **Weakening switches**: `allowAppleEvents` on macOS, `allowNestedUserNamespaces` and `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` on Linux each trade isolation for compatibility.

## Settings for a team

Administrators deliver keys through managed settings. `enabled`, `failIfUnavailable` and `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` together make the sandbox admin-required, and Claude Code then ignores repository settings that loosen it, such as a repo's `excludedCommands` or `allowedDomains`. `allowManagedDomainsOnly` and `allowManagedReadPathsOnly` lock network and read lists to managed values. Native Windows has no sandbox, so with `failIfUnavailable` set Claude Code exits there; move those users to WSL2 or a container.

## Limits Anthropic lists

The documentation says the sandbox reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary. The proxy decides on hostname and does not inspect TLS by default, so a broad entry like `github.com` can be an exfiltration path and domain fronting is possible. Allowing a Unix socket such as `/var/run/docker.sock` effectively hands over the host. Broad write rules to `$PATH` directories or shell startup files can lead to code running elsewhere.

## When to put the whole agent in a box

If MCP servers, hooks and file tools need a boundary too, the documentation points to running the Claude Code process itself in a container, VM or the sandbox runtime. Your options:

| Option | Covers file tools and MCP | Runs on | What it costs you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code Bash sandbox | No | Your machine | Little setup; shell commands only |
| Dev container | Yes | Your machine | Image upkeep; shares your laptop's CPU and RAM |
| Local VM | Yes | Your machine | Strong boundary; heavy on a laptop |
| Hosted sandbox service | Yes, for what you send it | Rented machines | Easy to scale; usage bills and your code leaves your hardware |
| Potluck sandbox | Commands sent to it | A spare Mac or Linux box your team owns | Early software; you run the pool |

Disclosure: Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without a Sengi account.

Potluck is not a replacement for Claude Code's settings. It is not a sandbox runtime of its own; it drives Tart on Apple silicon Macs and Kata, gVisor or Incus on Linux, and puts each sandbox on a machine that is not your laptop. On the OCI layer the default is no network at all. Trust still applies: the machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, and the machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

Create a pool with `potluck create friends` (the first time it prints a Tailscale login URL). `potluck invite carl --host` makes a code for someone sharing a machine, who runs `potluck host '<code>'`; `potluck doctor` and `potluck host --dry-run` show what will be shared first. Then:

```sh
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

`potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. To hand an agent sandbox tools, run `potluck --pool friends mcp`; see [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) and [agent sandboxes](/agent-sandbox).

## What makes Potluck different

- When the Bash sandbox is not enough, it uses the Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns instead of rented machines.
- Each command an agent sends lands in a fresh VM or sandbox, and the same pool can also run GitHub Actions jobs (run by hand so far, not yet daily in Potluck's own CI).
- Agents get sandbox tools over MCP with `potluck --pool friends mcp`.
- A lent Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer; on Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
- It is free and open source (Apache-2.0) and runs without a Sengi account.

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions, and if you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### Is the Claude Code sandbox on by default?

No. Turn it on with `/sandbox` in a session or set `sandbox.enabled` to true in a settings file.

### Does the sandbox stop Claude from reading my .env file?

Only for shell commands. The Read tool follows permission rules, so add a Read deny rule as well as a sandbox `denyRead` or `credentials` entry.

### Does the sandbox work on Windows?

Not natively; commands run unsandboxed there. Run Claude Code inside WSL2 to get it.

### What is dangerouslyDisableSandbox?

It is the parameter Claude uses to retry a failed command outside the sandbox. Set `allowUnsandboxedCommands` to false to make Claude Code ignore it.

### Is the sandbox a full security boundary?

Anthropic's documentation says no: the proxy filters by hostname without inspecting TLS, and broad allowlists or sockets can undo it. For a harder line, isolate the whole agent process.

### Does Potluck replace Claude Code's sandbox?

No. It gives agents fresh VMs or sandboxes on machines your team owns, over MCP or the `potluck sandbox` commands. Keep your permission rules either way.

### Is Potluck free?

Yes. It is open source under Apache-2.0, and you can read the code at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.
