# Coding Agent Sandboxing Guide: Containers vs gVisor vs microVMs (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/coding-agent-sandboxing-guide-containers-gvisor-vms-compared

**Short answer**: a plain container (Docker or Podman with the default runc runtime) shares the host kernel, so it is a packaging boundary, not a sandbox for code an agent writes. gVisor puts a user-space kernel between the agent and the host, and a microVM or full VM (Firecracker, Kata, Tart) gives the agent its own kernel, which is the strongest of the three. Then pick where the boundary runs: hosted platforms such as E2B, Modal and Daytona rent it to you, while self-hosting puts gVisor or a VM on hardware you already pay for. Potluck, a free, open-source (Apache-2.0) and early project, takes the self-hosted route. It runs each agent task in a fresh Tart VM on an Apple silicon Mac, or in a Kata or gVisor sandbox on Linux, on a team's idle machines. Per the Potluck docs, it caps macOS guests at two per Mac under Apple's licence.

## The isolation options at a glance

| Boundary | Kernel the agent talks to | What it stops | What it costs you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process sandbox (Seatbelt, Bubblewrap, Landlock, seccomp) | The host kernel, with rules | File and syscall access outside allowed paths | Rules are easy to get wrong; agents have been seen probing for gaps |
| Container (Docker or Podman, runc) | The host kernel, shared | Casual mistakes, dependency mess | A kernel bug or a bad mount reaches the host |
| gVisor | A user-space kernel that re-implements syscalls | Direct calls into the host kernel | Some software hits syscalls gVisor does not emulate the same way |
| microVM (Firecracker, Kata Containers) | Its own guest kernel on hardware virtualization | Kernel exploits reaching the host | Needs KVM; you manage images and networking yourself |
| Full VM (Tart on a Mac, Incus on Linux) | Its own full OS | Same as a microVM, and you get macOS | Slower to start, more memory per guest |

The order runs weakest to strongest. Every step up costs some start time and memory, and buys a smaller surface the agent can attack.

## Why a coding agent needs more than a container

A coding agent writes a command and runs it before you read it. It installs packages, runs test suites, starts servers and deletes files. Most of the time that is fine. The cases that hurt are the ordinary ones: a cleanup step with a bad path, an install script piped from an unknown host, a test that forks until the machine stalls, or a dependency that reads environment variables and sends them somewhere.

A container handles the dependency mess well. It does not handle a hostile or broken process well, because every syscall still lands in the host kernel. That is why the hosted sandbox vendors and the cloud providers all reach for gVisor or a VM when the code is untrusted. Treat agent-written code as untrusted even when the agent is yours.

Three things matter as much as the kernel boundary:

- **Network.** Default to no egress. Most real damage needs a way out, so a box that cannot reach the internet, your LAN or your tailnet is far safer than one that can.
- **Secrets.** A sandbox does not scrub the API keys you pass in. Give the agent only the tokens the task needs.
- **Lifetime.** A fresh sandbox per task means a bad run cannot leave something behind for the next one.

## Containers vs gVisor vs microVMs: how to choose

Ask how much you trust the code and what it needs to run.

- **Your own scripts that passed review:** a container is enough.
- **Agent-written code on Linux, mostly language tooling:** gVisor is a good default. It runs ordinary OCI images and fits into Docker or Podman as a runtime. Test your toolchain first, since a few programs behave differently under it.
- **Agent-written code that installs arbitrary packages or binaries, or anything you would call hostile:** use a VM boundary, Kata on Linux or a microVM platform.
- **Anything that needs macOS or Xcode:** a full macOS VM, which on Apple silicon means a tool like Tart. No container or gVisor option runs macOS.

## Hosted platforms vs your own machines

Once you know the boundary, decide who runs it. Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners; Potluck itself is a separate free project, so weigh this table with that in mind.

| Option | Isolation | Where it runs | Good at | Costs more or needs more work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E2B | Firecracker microVMs | Hosted; open source, self-hostable | Clean SDKs, fast start for short tasks | Usage billing adds up for long sessions |
| Modal | gVisor | Hosted only | GPUs and Python workloads | No self-hosting; images defined in its SDK |
| Daytona | Docker by default, Kata optional | Hosted or self-hosted | Persistent dev environments | You must opt into Kata for a VM boundary |
| Google Agent Sandbox | gVisor or Kata on Kubernetes | Your cluster | Warm pools, no new vendor | You run the Kubernetes cluster |
| DIY Firecracker or gVisor | Your choice | Your servers | Full control | You build images, networking, scheduling |
| Potluck | Tart VMs on Mac; Kata or gVisor on Linux | Macs and Linux boxes you already own | Fresh sandbox per task on idle hardware, macOS guests | Early; machines are shared desktops, not a fleet |

Hosted platforms win when you need many sandboxes at once, GPUs or no hardware to look after. Self-hosting wins when you already own the machines, need macOS, or do not want agent code and repo contents on someone else's servers. Potluck sits in the self-hosted column but does not ask you to build a fleet: it drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus on the computers your team already has.

## What Potluck checks before a machine takes work

`potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per sandbox size and joins the pool only when a size passes. `potluck doctor` shows what a machine can share, and `potluck host --dry-run` prints the plan without changing anything. The `--share` flag sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared; the Potluck docs give the default as 0.5.

For network isolation, `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On the OCI layer (Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor) the default is no network at all.

Be clear about the trust model. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, and the machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust. There are no promises; use it at your own risk.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

Create a pool on the machine that will run it. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

Ana runs `potluck join '<code>'` to use sandboxes. Carl runs `potluck host '<code>'` to share a machine, and `potluck host stop` when he wants it back. Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux.

Run a sandbox by hand:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

To hand sandboxes to an agent, run `potluck --pool friends mcp`, which is an MCP server exposing sandbox tools. More on that in [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) and [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines). If your coding-agent vendor offers self-hosted runners, `potluck agent-runner` runs them in fresh sandboxes. See also the [agent sandbox](/agent-sandbox) page.

## What makes Potluck different

- **It uses the Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns** instead of rented machines, so a gVisor, Kata or Tart boundary for agent code runs on hardware you have already paid for.
- **A Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer.** The sandbox ends, running VMs end and new work is refused, so lending a desktop does not mean losing it. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
- **One pool serves coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs,** each in a fresh VM or sandbox. A real Actions job has run through the runner broker by hand on a Mac (Tart) and on a Linux box (OCI with gVisor), though not yet daily in our own CI. See [GitHub Actions runner](/github-actions-runner).
- **Agents get sandbox tools over MCP,** and teammates and invited friends can lend machines to the same pool.
- **It is free and open source (Apache-2.0) and runs without a Sengi account.** It is not a hosted cloud, not a sandbox runtime of its own and not a cluster scheduler.

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it on real agent work and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### Is Docker safe enough for a coding agent?

Not on its own with the default runc runtime, because the container shares the host kernel. Add gVisor or Kata as the runtime, or use a VM, and turn off network access unless the task needs it.

### What is the difference between gVisor and a microVM?

gVisor intercepts the agent's syscalls with a user-space kernel, so the agent never calls the host kernel directly. A microVM such as Firecracker or Kata gives the agent its own guest kernel on hardware virtualization, which is a stronger boundary but needs KVM and more setup.

### Can I sandbox a coding agent on macOS?

Yes, with a macOS or Linux VM on an Apple silicon Mac using Tart, which is what Potluck drives. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac; see [Tart](/tart).

### Does a sandbox protect my API keys?

No. Anything you pass into the sandbox is readable by the code inside it, and with Potluck the machine running the VM can read it too, so pass only the keys the task needs.

### Can I lend Mac time to people outside my team?

Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine under Apple's licence; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

### How much does Potluck cost?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0. You supply the machines and their power.

### Is Potluck ready to replace a hosted sandbox platform?

Not for every team. It is early, it runs on shared desktops rather than a fleet, and Linux hand-back is only a time window today, so try it on non-critical agent work first.

---

Source: https://potluck.sh/blog/e2b-alternatives-self-hosted-ai-agent-sandboxes

# E2B Alternatives in November 2026: Self-Hosted Sandboxes for Coding Agents

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/e2b-alternatives-self-hosted-ai-agent-sandboxes

**Short answer**: Yes, you can self-host coding agent sandboxes instead of using E2B's cloud. As of November 2026 the main self-hosted routes are:

- E2B's own open-source runtime, either the single-machine Embed package or the full infra on a cluster
- OpenSandbox
- Microsandbox
- Docker Sandboxes, for an agent on one laptop
- Building directly on Firecracker or gVisor
- Potluck, which pools the Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns

Potluck is free and open source (Apache-2.0). It gives each agent a fresh VM or sandbox through Tart on Apple silicon or Kata and gVisor on Linux. It is early. Among the options in this post, it is the only one that lends idle machines across a team and offers macOS sandboxes, capped at two per Mac to match Apple's licence.

Disclosure: Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without a Sengi account.

## Self-hosted E2B alternatives compared

| Option | Where it runs | Isolation | More than one machine | macOS sandboxes | Who operates it |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E2B cloud (baseline) | E2B's cloud | Firecracker microVM | Yes, managed | No, Linux only | E2B |
| E2B Embed | One Linux machine with KVM | Firecracker microVM | No, single machine | No | You |
| E2B infra | Your cloud account | Firecracker microVM | Yes, via Terraform and Nomad | No | You |
| OpenSandbox | Your servers | Docker, Kubernetes or Firecracker | Yes, via Kubernetes | No | You |
| Microsandbox | A library on your machine | microVM | Scaling past one machine is your job | No, Linux guests | You |
| Docker Sandboxes (local) | Your laptop | microVM with its own Docker Engine | No | No, Linux guests | You |
| Firecracker or gVisor, DIY | Your hosts | What you build | What you build | No | You |
| Potluck | Macs and Linux boxes your team owns, pooled | Tart VMs on Mac; Kata or gVisor on Linux | Yes, a pool over Tailscale or your own tunnel | Yes, up to two per Mac | You and your teammates |

## What E2B does, and why teams self-host

E2B runs Linux sandboxes for AI agents on Firecracker microVMs in its own cloud. It has Python and JavaScript SDKs and per-second billing. It does stateful work well: sandboxes can pause with memory intact and be forked. If you want zero operations and a mature SDK, it is a strong default.

The searches that lead here ask for something else: sandboxes on hardware you control. The usual reasons are:

- Code, files and secrets should stay on your own machines.
- Teams want to stop paying per second for CPU they already own.
- Plan session limits get in the way of long agent runs.
- E2B sandboxes are Linux only, and some agents need macOS.

E2B's own self-host story has three levels:

- Embed packages the open-source runtime for a single machine.
- The full infra runs across machines with Packer, Terraform and Nomad.
- Running E2B inside your own cloud account is an enterprise option that E2B operates.

Daytona, often listed as an alternative, moved core development to a private codebase earlier this year. Its public repository says it is no longer maintained, so it is a weak choice if self-hosting is the point.

## The options, one by one

### E2B Embed and E2B infra

Use these if your code already talks to the E2B SDK and you want the same API on your hardware. Embed is the quick path, but it is one node. The cluster path is a real infrastructure project that you patch and scale yourself. If you want to keep E2B-style code and run it elsewhere, see [use the E2B SDK on your own machines](/blog/use-the-e2b-sdk-on-your-own-machines).

### OpenSandbox

OpenSandbox is an Apache-2.0 project from Alibaba. It runs agent sandboxes on Docker, Kubernetes or Firecracker, has SDKs in several languages, and supports MCP. It fits a platform team that already runs Kubernetes and wants a sandbox service of its own. You operate it as a platform, not a tool.

### Microsandbox

Microsandbox is an Apache-2.0 library that boots microVMs on your own machine, with no server or daemon. It runs on Linux with KVM or on an Apple silicon Mac, and it runs OCI images, which means Linux guests. Its maintainers still warn users to expect breaking changes. Spreading work across more than one machine is left to you.

### Docker Sandboxes

Docker Sandboxes run a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex in a microVM with its own Docker Engine, on your laptop, with no charge for local use. This is a good answer for one developer and one machine. It does not pool machines across a team.

### Firecracker or gVisor directly

Building on Firecracker or gVisor gives you full control and no vendor. The cost is engineering time. You build networking, image handling, lifecycle management and an API before an agent can use it.

### Potluck

Potluck takes a different approach from the rest of this list. It does not ask you to stand up sandbox servers. Instead it puts the idle Macs and Linux boxes your team already has into a pool. Each coding agent or GitHub Actions job gets a fresh VM or sandbox on one of them.

Potluck is not a sandbox runtime of its own. It drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus. It is also not a hosted cloud or a cluster scheduler.

An agent can use the pool in two ways:

- From the command line, to create a sandbox, run commands in it and remove it.
- Through an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools.

What Potluck does not give you matters if you came from E2B:

- It hands out fresh sandboxes that you create and remove. It is not a drop-in for E2B's pause-with-memory or fork.
- It is early.
- On Linux, handing a machine back to its owner works only as a time window today. On a Mac it happens when the owner returns.

More detail is on the [agent sandbox page](/agent-sandbox) and in [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines).

## How to choose

- **You use the E2B SDK and have one spare Linux server:** E2B Embed.
- **You run Kubernetes and want a sandbox platform:** OpenSandbox.
- **One developer, one laptop:** Docker Sandboxes or Microsandbox.
- **Unusual isolation needs and engineering time to spend:** Firecracker or gVisor directly.
- **Your team has Macs and Linux boxes that sit idle, and agents need Linux or macOS:** Potluck.
- **You want no operations at all, or you rely on memory-preserving pause and fork:** stay on E2B's cloud.

## What self-hosting costs you: trust and operations

Every self-hosted option moves responsibility to you. With Potluck that responsibility is spread across the people in the pool, so be clear about who can see what:

- The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets.
- The machine that runs a pool can read the commands and output that pass through it.
- Join only a pool whose owner you trust. Potluck is used at your own risk, with no promises.

You can check isolation yourself. `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On the OCI layer the default is no network at all.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that runs the pool, create it. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL. Then make an invite code for a friend who will share a machine:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host
```

On a spare Mac or Linux box, check what it can share, preview the plan, then join with the code:

```
potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'
```

Here is what `potluck host` does:

- It checks the machine, pulls the image and runs a quick conformance check per size.
- It joins the pool only when a size passes.
- By default it shares half the machine's cores and RAM (`--share` defaults to 0.5).
- `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux.

Run a sandbox:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

Give an agent sandbox tools over MCP with `potluck --pool friends mcp`. See [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) for a walkthrough.

## What makes Potluck different

- **It uses the Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns instead of rented machines.** For a team leaving per-second sandbox bills, the compute is hardware already on desks.
- **A Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer.** The sandbox ends, so lending a laptop does not cost its owner their workday.
- **One pool serves both coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs, each in a fresh VM or sandbox.** A real Actions job has been run through the runner broker by hand, on a Mac and on a Linux box, though not yet daily in our own CI. See [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).
- **Teammates and invited friends can lend machines to the same pool, and agents get sandbox tools over MCP.** No single server has to carry the load.
- **It is free and open source (Apache-2.0) and runs without a Sengi account.**

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### Is there a self-hosted alternative to E2B for coding agent sandboxes?

Yes. E2B Embed, E2B's infra, OpenSandbox, Microsandbox, Docker Sandboxes and Potluck all run sandboxes on hardware you control. Potluck is the one built around pooling a team's existing Macs and Linux boxes.

### Can I self-host E2B itself?

Yes. Embed runs E2B's open-source runtime on one Linux machine, and the full infra runs across machines with Terraform and Nomad. Running it in your own cloud account as a setup E2B operates is an enterprise option.

### Can a coding agent get a macOS sandbox without a hosted service?

With Potluck, yes, on an Apple silicon Mac running Tart. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending them to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and this is not legal advice.

### How does an agent use a Potluck sandbox?

Run `potluck --pool friends mcp` to expose sandbox tools to an MCP-capable agent. You can also script `potluck sandbox create`, then `potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a` and `potluck sandbox rm <id>` directly.

### Is it safe to run agent code on a teammate's machine?

Each job runs in a fresh VM or sandbox, and `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. The host machine can still read everything inside the VM, including secrets, so pool only with people you trust.

### What does Potluck cost?

Nothing. It is free, open-source software under Apache-2.0 and runs without a Sengi account.

### Does Potluck replace E2B's pause and fork?

No. Potluck hands out fresh sandboxes that you create and remove. If memory-preserving pause or fork is central to your agent, E2B's cloud covers that.

# GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runner on macOS and Linux: Install, config.sh, Ephemeral and JIT Runners (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/github-actions-self-hosted-runner-macos-install-official

**Short answer**: To install a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner on macOS 11.0 or later, or on Linux such as Ubuntu 20.04 or later, open Settings, then Actions, then Runners, then New self-hosted runner, run the download commands shown, then `./config.sh --url REPO_URL --token TOKEN` and `./run.sh`. The registration token expires after one hour (GitHub Docs, "Adding self-hosted runners"). For a single-use runner, add `--ephemeral` to `config.sh` or create a just-in-time (JIT) runner through the REST API; GitHub de-registers it after one job, and your own automation wipes the machine. A matched runner has 60 seconds to pick up a job, and a job with no runner fails after 24 hours (GitHub Docs, "Self-hosted runners reference"). On a Mac, clean-per-job means a macOS VM per job, and Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs per Mac you own. Potluck, an early open-source project, runs that VM-per-job step on machines you already own.

Each fact below names the GitHub Docs page it comes from, as read in November 2026.

## Requirements for a self-hosted runner machine

The GitHub Docs page "Self-hosted runners reference" lists:

- **macOS**: macOS 11.0 (Big Sur) or later.
- **Linux**: among others, Ubuntu 20.04 or later, Debian 10 or later, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 or later, Fedora 29 or later.
- **Architectures**: x64 on Linux, macOS and Windows; ARM64 is listed for the same systems and marked as public preview on that page.
- **Network**: outbound HTTPS on port 443 to the GitHub domains the page lists, and at least 70 kilobits per second upload and download.
- **Docker container actions and service containers**: these need a Linux runner with Docker installed. They do not run on a macOS runner.

The runner application itself needs few resources, so size the machine for your builds.

One warning from "Adding self-hosted runners": GitHub recommends self-hosted runners only for private repositories, because a pull request from a fork of a public repository can run code on your machine.

## Install a self-hosted runner on macOS

These steps follow "Adding self-hosted runners".

1. Open the repository, then Settings, then Actions, then Runners, then New self-hosted runner. For an organization, open the organization Settings and choose New runner, then New self-hosted runner. Only an organization owner can add an organization runner.
2. Select macOS and your architecture. On an Apple silicon Mac mini, that is ARM64.
3. Run the download and extract commands exactly as the page shows them. They carry the current runner version, so copy them from that page.
4. Register the runner with the URL and token from the same page:

```
./config.sh --url REPO_URL --token TOKEN
```

5. Start it:

```
./run.sh
```

When connected, the terminal prints "Connected to GitHub" and "Listening for Jobs", and the runner appears under Runners. On macOS and Linux you install it as a background service after adding it; GitHub covers that on "Configuring the self-hosted runner application as a service".

Target the runner by its labels:

```
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, macOS, ARM64]
```

## Install a self-hosted runner on Linux with config.sh and a registration token

The Linux steps are the same: choose Linux on the New self-hosted runner page, run its download commands, then `./config.sh --url REPO_URL --token TOKEN` and `./run.sh`. Because the token expires after one hour, a script that registers runners later has to fetch a fresh token through the REST API. "Self-hosted runners reference" lists the credentials that can do that: an access token with `repo` scope for private repositories, `public_repo` for public ones, `admin:org` for organizations, or a GitHub App with the administration or organization_self_hosted_runners permission.

If workflows use Docker container actions or service containers, install Docker on the Linux runner.

## Ephemeral self-hosted runners: the single-use lifecycle

The GitHub Docs concept page "Self-hosted runners" notes that self-hosted runners do not need a clean instance for every job. That also means nothing cleans up for you. An ephemeral runner is registered once and takes one job:

```
./config.sh --url ORG_URL --token TOKEN --ephemeral
```

Per "Self-hosted runners reference", the lifecycle is:

1. Register with `--ephemeral`.
2. GitHub assigns one job to that runner.
3. After the job, the GitHub Actions service de-registers the runner.
4. Your automation wipes the machine, or discards the VM or container, and registers a new runner with a new token.

GitHub recommends ephemeral runners for autoscaling and advises against autoscaling persistent runners, because in some cases a job can be sent to a persistent runner while it is shutting down. A clean environment per job also limits what one job leaves behind for the next. The same page asks you to forward ephemeral runner logs to external storage, since the machine and its logs are gone after the job.

## Just-in-time (JIT) runners through the REST API

Instead of `config.sh --ephemeral`, you can create ephemeral, just-in-time runners with the REST API, described on "REST API endpoints for self-hosted runners". The generate-jitconfig endpoint returns an encoded configuration that you pass to the runner at start with `./run.sh --jitconfig`. A JIT runner is single-use and skips the separate token and config step, which suits a script that boots a VM and starts one runner inside it.

## Routing, queueing and runner updates

From "Self-hosted runners reference":

- GitHub sends a job to an online, idle runner that matches its `runs-on` labels and groups. If that runner does not pick it up within 60 seconds, the job is re-queued.
- If no matching runner is online, the job waits, and fails after 24 hours in the queue.
- Runners update themselves by default, so every fresh VM or container image starts by updating. Register with `--disableupdate` and update the image on your own schedule.
- With updates off, update within 63 days of a new runner version, or GitHub stops assigning jobs to that runner.

## Ways to get a clean environment per job

The autoscaling routes below come from "Self-hosted runners reference", plus Potluck. All pair with ephemeral or JIT runners.

| Option | What it does well | What it needs from you |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent runner (`config.sh`, `run.sh`) | Simplest install, warm caches | Manual cleanup; jobs share one disk |
| `--ephemeral` with your own scripts | One job per registration | Wipe and re-register logic, token fetching, log forwarding |
| JIT runner via REST API | Single-use, no separate token step | Code that calls the API and boots a fresh machine |
| Actions Runner Controller (ARC) | GitHub's reference implementation, full lifecycle | A Kubernetes cluster and people to run it |
| Runner Scale Set Client (actions/scaleset) | Go module for VMs, containers and macOS | You write the provisioning |
| workflow_job webhook | Scaling built exactly as you want | Your own service; depends on timely webhook delivery |
| Potluck runner broker | Fresh Tart VM on a Mac, or gVisor or Kata sandbox on Linux, on machines you own | Early; run by hand so far, not yet daily in its makers' CI |

Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without a Sengi account.

## Self-hosted macOS runners with an ephemeral VM per job

ARC targets Kubernetes, which does not run macOS. On a Mac, the clean-per-job pattern is: boot a macOS VM from an image, start one ephemeral or JIT runner inside it, delete the VM after the job. Tart is a common way to run those VMs on Apple silicon. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so plan for two concurrent macOS jobs per Mac. Lending those VMs to your team is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice. See our [Tart page](/tart) and [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac](/blog/self-hosted-github-actions-runner-on-your-mac).

## Where Potluck fits

Potluck is free, open-source (Apache-2.0) software that runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on machines a team already owns, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. It drives Tart on an Apple silicon Mac and Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. It is not a sandbox runtime of its own, not a hosted cloud and not a cluster scheduler.

What works today: a real Actions job has been run through Potluck's runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine with gVisor. It is not yet in daily use in its makers' own CI. Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer; on Linux, hand-back to a returning owner works only as a time window today.

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including repository secrets, and the machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use it at your own risk. More on the [GitHub Actions runner page](/github-actions-runner) and in [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that runs the pool (the first `create` prints a Tailscale login URL):

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host
```

On the Mac mini or Linux box that will share:

```
potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'
```

`potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a conformance check per size and joins only when a size passes. `--share` (default 0.5) sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, and `potluck host stop` stops sharing. `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. To contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### How long is a self-hosted runner registration token valid?

One hour, according to the GitHub Docs page "Adding self-hosted runners". Automation that registers runners later should fetch a fresh token through the REST API.

### What is the difference between --ephemeral and a JIT runner?

Both take one job and are then removed. `--ephemeral` is a `config.sh` flag used with a registration token; a JIT runner gets an encoded config from the REST API and starts with `./run.sh --jitconfig`.

### Can a macOS self-hosted runner run Docker container actions?

No. "Self-hosted runners reference" says Docker container actions and service containers need a Linux machine with Docker installed.

### What happens if no self-hosted runner is online?

The job stays queued and fails after 24 hours, per "Self-hosted runners reference".

### How many macOS VMs can I run per Mac for ephemeral runners?

Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. This is not legal advice.

### Is Potluck ready to replace my CI runners?

Not yet. A real Actions job has run through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on Linux, but it is not in daily use in its makers' CI, and it is early software.

### Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted runners, but it runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

# Give Coding Agents Their Own Mac: macOS VMs on a Mac mini (2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/giving-coding-agents-their-own-mac-macos-vms

**Short answer**: one Apple silicon Mac mini can give coding agents two macOS VMs at a time, because Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own. Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac for the same reason. The usual way to do it is Tart: clone a fresh macOS VM for each task, run the agent in it headless, and delete the VM when the task ends. UTM suits people who want the VM in a window, and Lima is built around Linux guests. Potluck, an early, free and open-source (Apache-2.0) project, drives Tart on your Macs and Kata or gVisor on Linux, so an agent gets a fresh sandbox per task through a command line or an MCP server without you writing the VM lifecycle yourself.

## The options compared

Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account.

| Option | What it runs on a Mac | Best at | Disposable per task | How an agent gets in | Work you do |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tart | macOS and Linux VMs on Apple silicon | Headless, scripted macOS guests from registry images | Yes, if you clone and delete per task | Your own scripts around its exec command | Write and maintain the lifecycle scripts |
| UTM | macOS, Linux and Windows guests, with a GUI | Interactive use, trying an OS in a window | Possible, mostly by hand | You shell into the guest | More manual steps for automation |
| Lima | Linux VMs, often used for containers | Linux dev environments on a Mac | Yes, for Linux guests | Shell or container tools | Not the tool for a macOS guest |
| Hosted Macs (cloud or hosted runners) | Machines you rent | No hardware to look after | Depends on the provider | Provider's API or runner | You pay for rented time |
| Potluck | Tart guests on Macs, Kata or gVisor sandboxes on Linux | Fresh sandboxes for agents and Actions jobs on machines you own | Yes, each run in a fresh VM or sandbox | `potluck sandbox` commands or the MCP server | Install, create a pool, host a machine |

## Why an agent needs its own Mac

A coding agent that builds a Mac app, clicks through its UI or installs tools wants the whole machine. On your desktop it competes with you for the keyboard, the pointer and the front window, and it can reach your files, your keychain and your shell history. A macOS VM fixes both: the agent gets a desktop of its own, and when the task ends you throw the VM away so the next task starts clean.

A developer blog post from November 2026, about running a Mac card game's UI tests in a VM, describes the pattern well: Xcode and the source stay on the host, the host builds a Debug app, the app is copied into a headless macOS guest, and the agent drives it there and reads back a screenshot and the accessibility tree. The host Mac stays usable the whole time.

## The two-VM limit on a Mac mini

The number that shapes every plan is two. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac to match. A Mac mini therefore gives you at most two agent Macs at once. For more parallel macOS agents you need more Macs, and Linux sandboxes on other boxes can take the work that does not need macOS.

The licence also limits who uses those guests. Lending a macOS guest to your team or to invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

## Doing it by hand with Tart

Tart, from Cirrus Labs, is the most direct route. You install it with Homebrew, use `tart clone` to pull a macOS image from a container registry into a named VM, start it headless with `tart run`, and send commands into the guest with `tart exec`. Use the prebuilt images that include Tart's guest agent, since exec needs it; the vanilla images lack it. The images are large, so check free disk space first, and pick the macOS version your app needs as its minimum.

To make the VM disposable, clone a fresh copy from the base image for each task and delete it afterwards. That loop is what you end up scripting: create, wait for the desktop, copy the build in, run, collect output, delete. It works well, and you own every line of it. For more on Tart, see our [Tart page](/tart).

## UTM and Lima: where they fit

UTM is a good app for running macOS, Linux and Windows guests in a window on Apple silicon. It is the friendlier choice when a person sits in front of the VM. For an agent that needs a fresh guest every few minutes, you do more by hand than with Tart.

Lima is a solid way to run Linux VMs on a Mac, often as the base for containers. If your agent only needs a Linux shell, a Lima VM on the Mac mini is a fine sandbox. For a macOS guest, people reach for Tart or UTM instead.

## Making the VM safe, and what safe means

A fresh VM per task stops one task from leaving files or processes behind for the next. Beyond that:

- **Network.** Decide what the guest can reach. With Potluck, `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On Potluck's OCI layer on Linux, the default is no network at all.
- **Secrets.** The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including any secret you pass in. Give an agent only the tokens the task needs.
- **The person at the Mac.** On a desk Mac, Potluck ends a Mac sandbox when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. A Mac mini in a cupboard has nobody touching it, so it stays available.

## Start with Potluck

Potluck is early. On macOS or Linux, with no Go needed:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that runs the pool (the first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL), create the pool and make a code for a machine to share:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host
```

On the Mac mini you want to share, which needs Tart on Apple silicon, check it, look at the plan, then host:

```
potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'
```

`potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. `--share` (default 0.5) sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared. `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

Then create a sandbox, run a command in it and remove it:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

To give an agent sandbox tools directly, run `potluck --pool friends mcp`, an MCP server the agent connects to. There is more in [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp) and [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines). If you use a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners, `potluck agent-runner` runs them in fresh sandboxes.

## What makes Potluck different

- **It uses the Mac mini you already own.** Your agent's VMs run on Macs and Linux boxes the team already has, instead of rented machines.
- **A desk Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer.** You can lend a work Mac to agents when it is idle without losing it when you sit down. On Linux, hand-back is only a time window today.
- **One pool, a fresh VM or sandbox per run, for agents and CI.** The same machines serve coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs. A real Actions job has been run through the runner broker by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box; it is not yet daily in our own CI.
- **Agents get sandbox tools over MCP,** and teammates or invited friends can lend their own machines to the same pool.
- **Free and open source (Apache-2.0), no Sengi account needed.** It drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus rather than replacing them, and it is not a hosted cloud or a cluster scheduler.

## Try it early

Potluck is early, and its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues. The code is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck. For a wider view, read [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## Questions people ask

### How many macOS VMs can a coding agent use on one Mac mini?

Two at once. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac.

### Is Tart or UTM better for an AI agent sandbox?

Tart, for most agent setups, because it is built for headless, scripted guests and has a guest agent for running commands. UTM is better when a person wants to use the VM in a window.

### Can I use Lima to give an agent a macOS VM?

Lima is built around Linux guests. Use it when a Linux shell is enough, and use Tart or UTM when the agent needs macOS.

### Are secrets safe inside the agent's VM?

Not from the machine running it: that machine can read everything in the VM, including secrets, and a pool's machine can read commands and output passing through it. Pass in only what the task needs and join only pools whose owner you trust.

### Can the agent's VM reach my home or office network?

It depends on your setup. With Potluck, `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

### Can I rent out my Mac mini's macOS VMs?

No. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine, but selling Mac time to the public is not allowed under Apple's licence. This is not legal advice.

### Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck is free, open source under Apache-2.0, and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account.

# Local Alternatives to Cloud AI Coding Sandboxes (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/local-open-source-alternatives-cloud-ai-coding-sandboxes

**Short answer**: the local alternatives to cloud AI coding sandboxes such as E2B and Daytona are open-source tools that run the same kind of isolated box on hardware you control. The main ones are E2B's own open-source runtime, microsandbox, Hotcell, agent-sandbox for Kubernetes and agentbox, plus the runtimes underneath them: Firecracker, gVisor, Kata Containers, nsjail and bubblewrap. The software is free to use. You pay in hardware and in the hours it takes to run it. Potluck takes a different route: free, Apache-2.0 software that pools the Macs and Linux boxes a team already owns and gives each agent a fresh VM or sandbox on one of them, with GitHub Actions jobs served from the same pool. Potluck is early, and it is made by Sengi, a company that sells hosted GitHub Actions runners.

## Local alternatives at a glance

| Option | What it is | Isolation | Runs on | Where it needs more work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E2B open-source runtime | The runtime behind E2B's managed service | Firecracker microVMs | Cloud accounts you operate | You run the same distributed system E2B runs |
| microsandbox | Embeddable library, no long-running daemon | libkrun microVMs | Apple silicon Macs, Linux with KVM, Windows | You wire it into your own agent code |
| Hotcell | Sandbox layer with a key-swapping gateway on the host | Docker, Firecracker, Apple Virtualization | One Mac, Linux box or VM | Sized to one machine; non-HTTP credentials still have to be injected |
| agent-sandbox | Kubernetes resource and controller | gVisor or Kata via RuntimeClass | Any Kubernetes cluster | You need to run a cluster |
| agentbox | Container wrapper for one developer's agent | Docker plus an egress proxy and firewall | Your own machine | Container boundary, one developer |
| Firecracker, gVisor, Kata, nsjail, bubblewrap | Building blocks | microVM, user-space kernel, VM-backed containers, Linux namespaces | Linux | You build lifecycle, networking and cleanup yourself |
| Potluck | A pool of a team's own machines for agent sandboxes and Actions jobs | Tart on Apple silicon; Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux | Macs and Linux boxes you own, joined over Tailscale | Early; Linux hand-back is only a time window today |

## Why teams move agent sandboxes off the cloud

Managed sandboxes are the least work. One API call and a box appears, and someone else patches the kernels. That is worth a lot, and for a team with no spare hardware it is often the right call.

The reasons people search for local alternatives are usually three:

- **Where the code runs.** Some repositories cannot leave company machines because of a client contract or policy.
- **The meter.** One agent session is cheap. Many agents running all day on per-second billing adds up, especially when Macs and Linux boxes sit idle on desks.
- **Control.** You pick the image, the network rules and when a box dies.

Running locally does not make the model provider go away. Your prompts and code still go to whichever model the agent calls, unless you run the model yourself too.

## The options, one by one

### E2B's open-source runtime

The runtime behind E2B's managed service is open source. It runs Firecracker microVMs with snapshot, pause and resume, and can be deployed into cloud accounts you operate. It is the closest thing to self-hosted E2B, and the most operational work on this list.

### microsandbox

microsandbox runs OCI images in microVMs built on libkrun, as a library with no server. It works on Apple silicon Macs, Linux with KVM and Windows, has SDKs for several languages, and supports secrets that never enter the VM. Good for builders who want sandboxing inside their own program.

### Hotcell

Hotcell runs as many sandboxes as one machine can hold, using Docker, Firecracker on Linux with KVM, or Apple Virtualization on macOS. Its strength is credentials: each sandbox gets a short-lived token, and a gateway on the host swaps it for the real key. Its own documentation says credentials that do not travel in an HTTP header still have to be injected.

### agent-sandbox for Kubernetes

If agents already run on Kubernetes, agent-sandbox adds a Sandbox resource with templates and warm pools. Isolation comes from the cluster's RuntimeClass, usually gVisor or Kata. It is a good fit for platform teams and a heavy one for a team without a cluster.

### agentbox

agentbox wraps a coding agent in a Docker container with an egress proxy, and injects secrets through the proxy so the agent never sees them. Lightweight, and aimed at a single developer.

### The building blocks

Firecracker gives a separate guest kernel through KVM. gVisor puts a user-space kernel between the container and the host. Kata gives VM-backed containers that keep OCI and Kubernetes interfaces. nsjail and bubblewrap confine a Linux process with namespaces, mounts and syscall filters. All are solid, and none is a finished agent product: you write the lifecycle, mounts, network policy and cleanup. Agent harnesses such as OpenHands sit on top and still need one of these as the boundary.

### What about Daytona?

Daytona's README says core development moved to a private codebase and the public repository no longer gets updates. You can fork the last open release, but it is not a maintained local option.

## A different approach: pool the machines you already own

Every tool above answers "how do I isolate code on this machine or cluster?" Potluck answers a different question: "we have spare Macs and Linux boxes on desks; how do we put them to work for agents and CI?"

Potluck is not a sandbox runtime of its own. It drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus. It is not a hosted cloud and not a scheduler for clusters. One machine runs a pool, teammates and invited friends join it, and some of them lend machines to it. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure.

What that changes for the reader:

- **The Mac on someone's desk is usable.** A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer, and when an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
- **One pool, two jobs.** The same pool serves coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. A real Actions job has been run through the runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in our own CI. `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.
- **Agents get tools directly.** `potluck --pool friends mcp` is an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent. More in [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp).

## What a local sandbox still has to get right

Local does not mean safe by default. With Potluck, `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet, and on the OCI layer the default is no network at all.

Be clear about trust. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Potluck does not swap API keys behind a gateway the way Hotcell, microsandbox or agentbox aim to. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use it at your own risk.

For Macs, Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

## How to choose

| If you need | Start with |
|---|---|
| Self-hosted E2B at cloud scale | E2B's open-source runtime |
| A microVM library inside your own program | microsandbox |
| Real API keys never inside the sandbox, on one host | Hotcell |
| Sandboxes as Kubernetes resources | agent-sandbox |
| A quick container for one developer's agent | agentbox |
| Full control of every layer on Linux | Firecracker, gVisor, Kata, nsjail or bubblewrap |
| Agent sandboxes and Actions jobs on the team's spare Macs and Linux boxes | Potluck |

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that will run the pool, create it. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL.

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

Ana runs `potluck join '<code>'` to use sandboxes. Carl runs `potluck host '<code>'` to share a machine. Before that, `potluck doctor` shows what the machine can share and `potluck host --dry-run` prints the plan. `potluck host` checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. `--share` sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared (default 0.5, per the Potluck docs). `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac (see [Tart](/tart)), or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. Then try a sandbox:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

For a longer walk-through, read [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines) and [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## What makes Potluck different

- **It uses the machines you already own.** Instead of renting sandboxes, agents run on the team's idle Macs and Linux boxes, each in a fresh VM or sandbox.
- **A Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer**, so lending a desk machine does not mean giving it up.
- **One pool serves agents and CI.** Coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs come from the same pool, though Actions is not yet in daily use in our own CI.
- **Teammates and invited friends can lend machines to the same pool**, and agents reach it through sandbox tools over MCP.
- **It is free and open source (Apache-2.0)** and runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues. The source is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.

## Questions people ask

### What is the best local alternative to E2B?

For E2B's own architecture on cloud accounts you run, use E2B's open-source runtime. For one machine with keys kept out of the sandbox, look at Hotcell or microsandbox. For a pool of the team's own Macs and Linux boxes, try Potluck.

### Can I run AI coding sandboxes on a Mac?

Yes. microsandbox and Hotcell support Apple silicon, and Potluck runs macOS guests through Tart, capped at two per Mac to match Apple's licence.

### Do local sandboxes keep my code private?

They keep execution on machines you control. Code and prompts still go to the model provider the agent calls, and with Potluck the machine running a VM can read everything inside it.

### Does Potluck keep API keys out of the sandbox?

No, it does not claim to. The host machine can read secrets in a VM, so if key isolation is your main need, Hotcell, microsandbox or agentbox focus on it.

### Is Daytona still open source?

Its last open release can still be forked, but its README says development moved to a private codebase and the public code gets no further updates.

### Can Potluck run GitHub Actions jobs too?

A real Actions job has been run through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but not yet daily in our own CI. See [GitHub Actions runner](/github-actions-runner) for the current state.

### Is Potluck a hosted service?

No. It is free, open-source software you run yourself, and it needs no Sengi account.

# Open source sandbox for AI coding agents, self-hosted (2026): Claude Code sandboxing and your own hardware

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/open-source-sandboxes-ai-coding-agents

**Short answer:** In November 2026 you have two layers to choose from. The first is the sandbox built into Claude Code. It is off by default; you turn it on with `/sandbox`. It confines only the shell commands Claude runs: writes are limited to the working directory, and network access goes through a proxy that checks each host against an allowlist. The second layer puts the whole agent, or the commands it runs, inside a container or VM. Open-source tools for that second layer include Anthropic's sandbox runtime, OpenSandbox (Apache-2.0, on Docker or Kubernetes) and Potluck (Apache-2.0, free, early). Potluck runs each sandbox in a fresh VM or sandbox on Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns. Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners; Potluck itself is a separate free project.

## The options compared

| Option | What it isolates | Where it runs | Open source | Where it costs more or needs more work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code Bash sandbox | Shell commands and their child processes | Your own machine: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2 | Built on Anthropic's open-source sandbox runtime | File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it; reads most of your disk by default |
| Anthropic sandbox runtime around the whole process | The Claude Code process itself | Your own machine | Yes | You write and maintain the filesystem and network policy |
| Dev container or local VM | Everything inside the container or VM | Your own machine | Depends on the tool | Uses your laptop's cores and RAM; setup per project |
| OpenSandbox | Agent commands, code interpreters, browsers | Your servers on Docker or Kubernetes; gVisor, Kata or Firecracker | Yes, Apache-2.0 | You run and scale the servers |
| E2B, Daytona | Agent code in hosted sandboxes | The vendor's cloud, with an open-source core | Partly | Pay as you go; code runs on someone else's machines |
| Potluck | Each job in a fresh VM or sandbox | Spare Macs (Tart) and Linux boxes (Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor) on your team | Yes, Apache-2.0 | Early; the host machine can read what runs on it |

The hosted services do well when you want no machines to look after. The self-hosted options do well when you already have hardware and want code to stay on it.

## What the Claude Code sandbox restricts

Anthropic's Claude Code documentation describes the Bash sandbox as a boundary that the operating system enforces around shell commands. On macOS it uses Seatbelt, which ships with the system. On Linux and WSL2 it needs bubblewrap and socat from your package manager. On native Windows, commands run unsandboxed, so the docs point Windows users to WSL2.

With it on, by default:

- **Writes** go only to the working directory, a per-user temp directory and directories you added. Claude Code's own settings, hooks directories and shell startup files stay write-protected.
- **Reads** cover most of the machine, including `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws/credentials`. You close that with `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` or the `sandbox.credentials` block.
- **Network** has no direct route out. Traffic goes through a local proxy that checks each hostname against `allowedDomains`, which starts empty. Tools that ignore proxy variables, such as plain `ssh` and most database drivers, cannot connect at all.
- **Environment variables** are inherited, secrets included, unless you deny or mask them.

To turn it on, run `/sandbox` in a session and pick auto-allow or regular permissions. To turn it on everywhere, set `sandbox.enabled` to `true` in `~/.claude/settings.json`. To check it works, ask Claude (not the `!` prompt) to run `touch ~/sandbox-probe`; inside the sandbox it should fail.

## What runs outside it

This is the part people miss. The Claude Code docs list what the Bash sandbox does not cover:

- The built-in Read, Edit, Write, WebFetch and WebSearch tools, which follow permission rules instead.
- Hooks, local MCP servers, LSP servers and helper commands, which run with your full access.
- Commands you type yourself at the `!` prompt, in most sessions.
- Commands matched by `excludedCommands`, and commands Claude retries unsandboxed after a failure. Setting `allowUnsandboxedCommands` to `false` turns that retry off.

The docs also say plainly that the sandbox reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary, and that the proxy does not inspect TLS by default. Their advice for putting everything behind one boundary is to run the Claude Code process itself in a container, a VM or the sandbox runtime.

Some common tools also fail inside it: `docker`, jest with watchman, and on Linux, Chromium and rootless Podman. Each workaround gives up some isolation.

## How to run Claude Code in a sandbox on your own computer

Pick by what you want to protect:

1. **Protect your files and network from stray shell commands.** Turn on `/sandbox`, deny reads of credential paths, keep `allowedDomains` short, and turn off unsandboxed retries. This costs nothing and stays on your laptop.
2. **Protect your whole machine from the agent.** Run Claude Code inside a dev container, a local VM or the sandbox runtime. Everything the agent starts is inside the boundary, but it shares your laptop's CPU and memory.
3. **Keep the agent's commands off your laptop entirely.** Send the commands to a throwaway sandbox on another machine. This is where OpenSandbox, the hosted services and Potluck sit.

Many teams do 1 and 3 together: the built-in sandbox for local work, and a separate box for builds, tests and anything that needs network access you would not grant on your own machine.

## Open-source, self-hosted sandboxes for AI coding agents

**OpenSandbox** manages the sandbox lifecycle (start, monitor, pause, terminate) on Docker for local testing and Kubernetes for production. It ships SDKs in several languages, lets you choose gVisor, Kata Containers or Firecracker for isolation, and has an MCP server so Claude Code or Cursor can call it. You run and scale the servers yourself.

**Anthropic's sandbox runtime** is the open-source package the Claude Code sandbox is built on. You can use it on its own to wrap the whole Claude Code process on one machine.

**Potluck** takes a different angle: it does not ship its own sandbox runtime. It drives Tart on Apple silicon Macs, and Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux (Incus is also supported), and it pools the idle machines a team already owns. Each job gets a fresh VM or sandbox. It runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account. It is not a hosted cloud and not a scheduler for clusters.

What Potluck does for agents today:

- `potluck --pool friends mcp` runs an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent, so Claude Code can run commands in a pooled sandbox instead of on your laptop. More in [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp).
- `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.
- On the OCI layer the default is no network at all, and `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

What to know before you use it:

- The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, secrets included. The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust.
- A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
- Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac (Potluck facts). Lending them to your team is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not. This is not legal advice.

See [the agent sandbox page](/agent-sandbox) and [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines) for more.

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that will run the pool:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

The first `create` prints a Tailscale login URL. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure. Ana runs `potluck join '<code>'` to use sandboxes. Carl first checks his spare box with `potluck doctor` and `potluck host --dry-run`, then runs `potluck host '<code>'`. That checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size, and joins only when a size passes. By default `--share` is 0.5, so half the cores and RAM are shared (Potluck facts). `potluck host stop` ends sharing.

A worked example from Ana's laptop:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

To hand the pool to Claude Code, register `potluck --pool friends mcp` as an MCP server. For Mac specifics, see [Tart](/tart); for spreading work over several boxes, see [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

## Questions people ask

### Is the Claude Code sandbox on by default?

No. Anthropic's docs say it is off until you run `/sandbox` or set `sandbox.enabled` to `true` in a settings file.

### Does the Claude Code sandbox cover file edits and MCP servers?

No. It covers shell commands and their child processes. The Read, Edit and Write tools, hooks and local MCP servers run outside it.

### What is an open-source sandbox for AI coding agents I can run on my own hardware?

Anthropic's sandbox runtime for one machine, OpenSandbox on your own Docker or Kubernetes servers, and Potluck for pooling a team's spare Macs and Linux boxes. All are open source; you supply the hardware.

### Can I sandbox Claude Code on Windows?

The Claude Code docs say native Windows runs commands unsandboxed and recommend WSL2. To share a machine in a Potluck pool you need an Apple silicon Mac or a Linux box.

### Does Potluck cost anything or need a Sengi account?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0, and it runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account. Sengi, its maker, sells hosted GitHub Actions runners as a separate product.

### Can the person who hosts my sandbox see my code?

Yes. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, so join only pools whose owners you trust.

### Does Potluck run GitHub Actions too?

A real Actions job has been run through the runner broker by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in Potluck's own CI. See [the GitHub Actions runner page](/github-actions-runner).

# Open-Source Self-Hosted Coding Agents and CI on Your Own Machines (November 2026)

Published 2026-11-24. https://potluck.sh/blog/open-source-self-hosted-coding-agents-and-ci

**Short answer**: To run coding agents and CI jobs on machines you already own with open-source software, you need two pieces: an agent and a safe place to run it and your builds. For the agent, OpenHands and OpenCode are MIT-licensed according to their repositories, and Cline's CLI, Desktop and VS Code surfaces are Apache-2.0 according to its repository. For the machines, Potluck, free and Apache-2.0, made by Sengi, Inc., pools a team's idle Macs and Linux boxes and runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on them, each in a fresh VM or sandbox, with at most two macOS guests per Mac (Apple's licence). Potluck is early: a real Actions job has gone through it by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but it does not yet run daily in its makers' own CI.

## Two jobs: the agent, and the machine it runs on

Most pages about self-hosted coding agents compare agents. That is half the question. The searches behind this post ask for something that runs agents and CI jobs on machines you already own, which splits into:

- **The agent or harness.** The program that reads code, calls a model and runs commands. OpenHands, OpenCode, Cline, Coder Agents, or a CLI such as Claude Code or Codex.
- **The execution layer.** The machine, VM or sandbox where those commands and your CI jobs actually run, and what that box can reach.

An agent on your laptop runs with your shell, your files and your network. A CI job on a self-hosted runner runs on whatever host you installed it on. Neither is isolated unless you add isolation. Potluck works on the second job: it turns spare Macs and Linux boxes into a pool that hands out fresh VMs and sandboxes, and it drives existing runtimes (Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus) instead of shipping its own.

## The options at a glance (November 2026)

Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project that runs without Sengi or a Sengi account. Licences below are as stated by each project's own repository or docs.

| Option | What it is | Runs on your machines | Licence | Where it needs more work or costs more |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agent CLI on a box you own, in tmux | Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode on a Linux machine, kept alive with tmux over SSH | Execution, clone, credentials | Depends on the CLI; Codex CLI is Apache 2.0 | One shared checkout, sessions lost on reboot, no isolation from the host |
| OpenHands | Agent harness with a web UI; each conversation can get its own Docker container | Harness, UI, execution | MIT | You run Docker, upgrades and access control; its docs say the UI is unauthenticated as installed |
| OpenCode | Agent CLI with a headless server mode and local model support | CLI and execution | MIT | Isolation is whatever machine you start it on |
| Cline CLI, Desktop, VS Code | Agent surfaces using your own provider or a local runtime | Execution, credentials | Apache-2.0; the JetBrains plugin is not open source | Its docs say telemetry is on by default; check the approval defaults |
| Coder Agents | Agent platform for your data center or cloud account | Platform and execution | AGPL v3 | A platform to deploy and operate |
| GitHub's self-hosted runner | GitHub's runner program installed on a machine you own | Actions jobs | Open source, published by GitHub | Jobs run on the host itself unless you add your own VM or container wrapping and cleanup |
| Potluck | Pools owned Macs and Linux boxes; Actions jobs and agents in fresh VMs or sandboxes | Actions jobs, agent sandboxes, vendor agent runners | Apache-2.0 | Early; Linux hand-back only as a time window; Actions not yet daily in its makers' CI |
| Hosted runners (GitHub-hosted, Sengi and others) | Someone else's machines, paid by use | Nothing | Not self-hosted | Recurring cost; in exchange there is no hardware to maintain |

These combine. A team can run OpenCode or OpenHands as the agent and point its command execution at Potluck sandboxes, and keep GitHub's runner for some jobs while moving others to fresh VMs.

## How Potluck plugs into agents and CI

Potluck exposes the pool in four ways.

**Sandboxes from the command line.** `potluck sandbox create` prints an id, `potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a` runs a command inside it, and `potluck sandbox rm <id>` removes it. Any script or agent that can run a shell command can use these. More in [run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines](/blog/run-coding-agents-in-a-sandbox-on-your-own-machines) and on the [agent sandbox](/agent-sandbox) page.

**An MCP server for agents.** `potluck --pool friends mcp` starts an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent, so an agent that speaks MCP can create a box, run commands in it and throw it away. See [give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP](/blog/give-your-ai-agent-a-sandbox-over-mcp).

**Vendor agent runners.** `potluck agent-runner` runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes, so a hosted agent product that supports self-hosted runners executes on your hardware instead of a long-lived host.

**GitHub Actions.** A runner broker sends Actions jobs to fresh VMs or sandboxes. As of today a real Actions job has been run through it, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine using OCI with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in our own CI, so treat it as something to try, not something to move your release pipeline onto. Details on the [GitHub Actions runner](/github-actions-runner) page and in [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac](/blog/self-hosted-github-actions-runner-on-your-mac).

## What stays on your machines, and what still leaves

Self-hosting execution keeps the repository clone, build outputs and the credentials the job uses on hardware you own. It does not, by itself, keep everything local:

- **The model request.** Where prompts and the file contents an agent reads are sent is set by the agent's own configuration. With a hosted model they go to that provider. OpenHands, OpenCode and Cline each document local model servers such as Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM if prompts must stay in your network.
- **The host can read the guest.** In Potluck, the machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs a pool can read the commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and keep production secrets out of pools that include machines you do not control.
- **Network reach.** Whatever a box can reach, an agent in it can reach. `potluck isolation test <size>` checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On the OCI layer the default is no network at all, which also means a job that needs to download packages needs network you choose to give it.

There are no promises here: use it at your own risk, and verify the boundaries you care about on your own setup.

## What each machine needs

- **Mac:** Tart on an Apple silicon Mac. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice. See the [Tart](/tart) page.
- **Linux:** Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor.
- **Sharing:** `--share` sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, and Potluck's default is 0.5, half the machine.
- **Taking a machine back:** a Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.

Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure. For a longer walkthrough of a mixed pool, see [pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents](/blog/pool-spare-macs-and-linux-boxes-for-builds-and-agents).

## How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach
```

On the machine that runs the pool:

```
potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host
```

The first `potluck create` prints a Tailscale login URL. `potluck invite ana` makes a code for a friend who runs sandboxes; `potluck invite carl --host` makes a code for a friend who shares a machine.

A friend who wants sandboxes runs `potluck join '<code>'`. A friend sharing a machine first runs `potluck doctor` to see what it can share and `potluck host --dry-run` to print the plan, then `potluck host '<code>'`. That checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. `potluck host stop` stops sharing.

Then try a box:

```
potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>
```

## Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks: a machine that fails the conformance check, a runner job that hangs, an agent that cannot reach its sandbox. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions with what you ran and what happened. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues. The source is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.

## Questions people ask

### What open-source tools run coding agents and CI jobs on machines I already own?

For the agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Cline's open-source surfaces and Coder Agents all run on your own hardware. For execution, GitHub's self-hosted runner runs Actions jobs on a host you own, and Potluck runs Actions jobs and coding agents in fresh VMs or sandboxes across a pool of your Macs and Linux boxes.

### Is Potluck a coding agent?

No. Potluck gives agents and CI jobs a place to run: fresh sandboxes from the command line, an MCP server with sandbox tools, and `potluck agent-runner` for a vendor's self-hosted runners. You bring the agent.

### Can I run an open-source coding agent fully locally?

The agent and its commands can run entirely on your machines. The model request leaves unless you point the agent at a local model server, which OpenHands, OpenCode and Cline each document; check the agent's telemetry and update settings too.

### Does Potluck run GitHub Actions jobs today?

A real Actions job has been run through its runner broker by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box with OCI and gVisor. It is not yet running daily in its makers' own CI, so it is ready to try, not to depend on.

### What does Potluck cost?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0, and it runs without Sengi or a Sengi account. Your cost is the machines you already own.

### Can I lend my Mac to friends for builds?

Yes, to your team or invited friends, with at most two macOS guests per Mac as Apple's licence allows. Selling Mac time to the public or pooling iOS Simulator time is not allowed; this is not legal advice.

### Is my code safe on someone else's machine?

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, and the pool's machine can read commands and output. Join only pools whose owner you trust, and keep secrets you cannot afford to expose out of shared pools.

### Do I need Kubernetes?

No. Potluck is not a cluster scheduler; it runs on individual Macs and Linux boxes with Tart, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor.
